The House resumed, from Friday, April 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-22, intituled Canadian Football Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate I suppose it is necessary to point out to members on the other side of the House that it is they who introduced this measure, and until they provide more evidence than has been provided by government speakers so far, it is in the public interest to determine whether or not this legislation is really necessary, to determine whether the fears which have been expressed by people outside the House and by government spokesmen inside the House are well founded. Essentially, we have to ask ourselves whether or not the government has so far produced any evidence which supports the suggestion that its fears are grounded on fact, not just on fancy.
It is important for all hon. members, and especially for those people we represent in consituencies across Canada, to recognize that it is the duty of the government to propose legislation. That is a proper function of government. But it is also the duty of the government to indicate in debate the reasons for which legislation has been introduced and the evidence supporting those reasons. I think probably hon. members of this House on both sides and in all parties, would call themselves Canadian nationalists in what I think is the best sense of that word. However, I do not think, with respect, it is enough for the government to presume upon that very natural instinct on the part of members of parliament of Canada by asking them on that basis-after all we are all interested in the national wellbeing of our country-to pass this bill without examination because the government tells us this is essential to the maintenance of our national identity.
Some government members may say the government has not gone quite that far. I am glad that some of them feel that government has not as this would indicate that they have not completely lost their own faculty for looking critically at this legislation and recognizing that we are really not talking about a matter of maintaining Canadian national identity. If I thought that was the issue I would say so, but no doubt if it were the issue there would be some pretty strong evidence to support it. What we are being asked to believe is that the entry of a WFL team in the city of Toronto is going to break up the Canadian Football League. We are also being asked to believe that should that happen the playing of Canadian football in this country will cease. We are also being asked to take from those propositions the assumption that this somehow, or in some way, will seriously impair our sense of being Canadian.
There has been a lot of talk about the role of Canadian football in keeping this country together, perhaps not so much in the House as outside the House, but this has to be taken in perspective. I, for one, along with many of my school mates, grew up in a city where we played American football in highschool because the university team had to play in an American football league. The school board was asked whether teams playing football in highschool could switch to the American rules in order that the talent coming to the university from the highschools would be better prepared to play in that league in which the university played.
Many of us also played Canadian football in weekend leagues at the same time we were playing American foot-
April 22, 1974

ball in the highschool league. In those days we did not have a Vancouver team in the Canadian Football League. We also played other sports, including English rugby and soccer. We did not play much hockey as there was not very much ice in Vancouver in those days. We played a mix of sports, and I think most of us have grown into pretty strong Canadian nationalists. I do not believe for one minute that I was somehow robbed of my right or chance to be a Canadian because I did not have imposed upon me a solid dose of Canadian football and nothing else during my so-called formative years.
It is also interesting that when we talk about the role of sports in Canada it seems we have been speaking for a number of years now about the importance of the government's role in assisting amateur sports. Some figures have been bandied about in respect of the nearly quarter of a million young people playing football in this country, but how many adults play Canadian football in this country after they leave school? Canadian football in that sense is certainly not as national a game as some other sports. I think there is no question that probably far more adults play hockey for recreation long after they leave school, than play Canadian football. I have not the figures but perhaps some government speaker will provide them during this debate. I suggest that soccer is another game which many more adults play long after they leave school than play Canadian football. I suggest also that the same is true of English rugby. It is not surprising that this is true because football, as such, has not been a game which has been easily converted into an amateur type sport to be taken up on an informal basis after you get away from the rigorous discipline of school or juvenile leagues.
When we talk about the position of Canadian football in sports for Canadians I think it is important to put it into perspective. As I say, I played Canadian football. I think it is a good game and, in some respects, its rules are superior to American rules, despite the fact that they are very similar. I would like to see young Canadians play not only Canadian football but soccer, rugby and hockey as much as possible. That does not mean we should denigrate in any way other individual sports which perhaps in the long run are more useful to the individual as they can be played for many years and provide a great deal of pleasure, and good healthful recreation, to persons of middle and older years.
I should point out also that when we are talking about government assistance and getting more and more people to participate in Canadian sports, in my own province and in my own city field hockey is now a major amateur sport, amateur in the best sense of the word, as is English rugby and soccer. When we talk about the government making a move to assist in the growth of Canadian football, to which I have no objection, I just hope that these other sports which are very much a part of the sports fabric of this country will not be neglected.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I did not identify the hon. member who made the lively interjection, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay). I did not feel that it was necessary to identify him because all regular readers of Hansard would know immediately of whom I was speaking. However, I apologize to the hon. member for not identifying him earlier. He is very identifiable, Mr. Speaker. He is always a delight and makes a great contribution to debates in this House.
As I was saying, I think one of the most significant contributions made to this debate was that of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). First of all, the hon. member said that we should not have to discuss the issue of football at this time and then enumerated other matters which are of greater importance to which I referred a few moments ago.
The hon. member for Greenwood, in a speech which I think every member of this House should read because it is pretty succinct and gets down to the nub of the issue, brought forward another reason for opposition to this bill, with which I agree, namely the question of the constitutionality of the bill. This is an aspect to which no speaker on the government side has directed his mind. As recorded at page 1593 of Hansard for Friday April 19, the hon. member for Greenwood said:
I would have thought that the regulation of sport generally was a matter for the provinces under property and civil rights and a matter of local and private nature.
On the same page he points out the second reason for worrying about the constitutionality of this:
Does it depend on peace, order or good government, the opening words of section 91? To me that is a nonsensical suggestion. That particular power relates to times of emergency. What emergency requires us to decide whether the Northmen play football in Toronto or do not play football in Toronto?
Of course, when one looks at the constitutionality of a bill one must consider the trade and commerce clause in the constitution. My hon. friend, the hon. member for Greenwood said this, again record on the same page:
It might be thought to be justified under the heading of trade and commerce. I know that is a complex subject and there are numerous cases, none of them clear. From my reading I have not been able to discover any case that justifies the suggestion that to allow someone to come across the border to play football, to play a musical instrument, albeit they are playing for money, is a matter of trade and commerce of such dimensions that it would justify legislation here on issues of trade and commerce.
The hon. member continues to cite a real problem which ought to jump out at all hon. members and when regard is taken of the penal provisions in this bill. He very correctly draws the attention of this House to this aspect of the bill. As recorded at page 1592 of Hansard, he asks this question:
Is it criminal law? Some clauses appear in the bill as if criminal law were included in this bill on purpose. This is an indication of the completely unconstitutional nature of the bill because criminal law certainly is a power that the federal government has but it cannot be used to justify interference in a field where the government has no right to be.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Greenwood has very properly brought a serious issue before this

House, one to which at least at this date the government has not addressed its mind in this debate.
There is another point, and I was pleased to see that the hon. member for Greenwood has alluded to it. It has been alluded to by other speakers here and by people generally outside the House. He said:
A basic right is involved here, that is the right of people to choose for themselves, unless there is some very good reason why they should not be allowed to and such reasons do not exist in the present case, what they want to watch on television or hear on radio. There is no reason why the consumer, that is the viewer who wants to view football directly or through any other means, should not have the widest possible choice, and if that choice involves some degree of American importation-and it does now and will continue to do so-so what? No nationalist rule compels us to say that we are going to shut our doors to seeing things, hearing them and enjoying them because they come from some other part of the world.
I think we can get too caught up on the fact that this bill relates to Canadian football and forget exactly what kind of precedent we are setting here. It is a little like saying that what Canada needs is to decide on what national game we want and have the government so state and disallow all other games. It is like saying that we will play this one game because it is Canadian. That would be preposterous.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare said this was analogous to what we have done under the Foreign Investment Review Act. I wonder if it is. Surely, all we did under the Foreign Investment Review Act was say that if someone wishes to have a business in Canada, no matter what kind it may be, we will ensure that there is sufficient Canadian control and Canadian ownership so that there is a greater probability of that business acting as a good corporate Canadian citizen. But we never said in that bill that there are some kinds of businesses one cannot have. This surely is what the bill in front of us is doing. It is saying there are some kinds of sport which one cannot have. If somebody plays American football in one city or in two or three, how does it become such a serious threat to our national way of life that it should be outlawed?
This is not the same as the situation in respect of banks or trust companies or the stopping of the sale of a company which controls the extraction of uranium. It is not something which goes to the heart of the national interest as has been propounded.
I think we must put Canadian football in some sort of perspective. As I have said, I have played the game of Canadian football and hope to watch it for the rest of my life but frankly I do not believe, unless there are better reasons than have been given so far, that we need this kind of legislation to protect Canadian football. If there are a quarter of a million young people playing this game right now, and if steps will be taken to increase that number to 500,000 or 600,000, as the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) said in Friday's debate, surely to goodness we will be producing so may competent football players, so much Canadian football will be played, that there would be no difficulty in a commercial league existing in this country in a good, healthy way.
Another question one should ask oneself is: given the amount of professional football that is being played south
April 22, 1974

of the border, can anyone seriously think that Canadian players will not be induced to play in the United States if they are good enough and if they are paid enough? It is very difficult to see exactly how the bill before us will stop that sort of thing from taking place. Surely, the way to combat that kind of thing is to have a heck of a good Canadian league, do everything you can to promote it in the schools, play the game well, play it constantly, and do one more thing which is very important, namely, have people play it after they leave school so that it becomes an integral part of our adult amateur sports scene. If it does not do that, then all of this is being done just to have a commercial league, and I for one am not prepared to see the government put all its effort into assisting the commercial side of a sport in which a large number of our people do not engage in their adult years.
The hon. member for Greenwood spoke about Canadian unity. I should like to quote him from Hansard of April 19, page 1592, where he is reported as having said the following:
My fourth point is that the pretence that this legislation is essential to defend Canadian culture and unity, to my mind at least, is completely phoney. Canadian culture and unity do not depend upon which of two types of football are played or watched in Canada,
I will not go quite as far as the hon. member did because I do not believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare or, for that matter, some members of the government who have got themselves in this jam, did so on a phoney basis. It may be phoney in fact but I do not think that was their intent. But I am concerned about the suggestion that to even question this bill makes your own Canadian nationalism, Canadian identity or Canadian patriotism suspect. What is it that has suddenly put the Canadian national identity in peril? Is it the WFL team playing in Toronto? Somehow that seems rather absurd. We have gone through much peril since the time our ancestors, French, English and otherwise, arrived on this continent and hammered out a good country, contrary to many people who said it could not be done and contrary, as some people would put it, to the law of economics and the commonsense of geography. We have done that and we are in the House today debating because this country's sense of identity is not on the skids; this country's nationalism, our sense of who we are and what we are, is very much alive. I know that all hon. members, deep down in their hearts, realize that.
Throughout our history there have been those who have constantly told us that we would not make it, that we would slide into an abyss, that we would divide and separate among ourselves and that we would be gobbled up by the American colossus or we would be lost to materialism or some other undesirable event. I grew up reading learned essays by people who constantly repeated that we have no Canadian identity, that we have no national purpose, that somehow or other we do not know who we are or what we are. There are always some who, lacking anything else to write about, create issues. They transport them into the centre of academic discussions and, having invented an ailment that does not exist, they spend the rest of their careers prescribing methods to cure it. These people really do not do much harm, but I am sorry they do not apply their talents to real problems. Frankly, I think there is something peculiar in the Minis-

The hon. member for York West suggested that it was in the public interest to pass this bill. That is what he appears to have said, and I refer to Hansard of last Friday at page 1585 where he is reported to have said:
You know, filibuster can be a very effective technique for the opposition in times of majority government. It can be used to keep the majority from legislating something that the opposition feels is not in the public interest.
I take it from that the hon. member for York West believes that this bill is in the public interest. Where is the evidence that the Canadian Football League is really threatened?
The hon. member for York West said, as I have mentioned earlier in my speech, that in a few years there will be 500,000 to 600,000 young Canadians playing football. According to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, there will be help from his department, and with all this help and with that kind of growth one wonders why the CFL is in so much trouble. I say that even if I cannot see the reasons why the Canadian game is in trouble, it is incumbent upon the government to tell me why it is in trouble, not just to tell me, as the minister did, that it is a gut issue. He should tell me why we have to take this rather extraordinary step to save the CFL and apparently our sense of Canadian identity.
As I said earlier it is incumbent upon the government which proposed this bill to give me the evidence upon which they base their assertion that it will be the end of the Canadian Football League if we do not pass this bill. Surely, that is their theory, and that is what they think will happen if this team comes to Toronto, if this Mr. whatever-his-name-is who is supposed to be a millionaire and is apparently so important in the world of sports these days, brings this team to Toronto. I could not care a fig for the owner of this American team. I do not give a hoot whether or not they play. What I am concerned about is whether or not this is the way we should deal with it. People in Canada, and people in Toronto in particular, want to watch that team play and unless you can give me very good reasons why they should not, then I am afraid I have to say: let them play.
I am certainly no spokesman for the owners of that team. Frankly I am not much interested in professional football. I do not think that in terms of the actual state of health of most Canadians, professional football contributes very much to it. Whether it is the American stations we watch or whether we go to the stadium to watch the Canadian game, it is entertainment. I do not think it does very much for anyone's health except those who are playing-they are probably in pretty good shape.

Some of the most important things in our lives are emotional. There is a time to appeal to emotion. If we lived lives in which we did not appeal to emotion, and if we acted in a way that did not recognize the emotional sides of our lives, we would live a dry, rigid, dusty existence, without humanity and compassion. After letting this emotional response work through our visceral innards, we should apply our minds to the real issue. Really, there are only two questions that need to be asked. Second, do we really believe that the only way to preserve Canadian football is to prohibit a game that happens to have its rules made outside of the geographic boundaries of this country. I ask all members to ask themselves these questions. When we read the first paragraph of the preamble to this bill, we realize that one of the premises on which this government based the drafting of this bill is the following:
-football has an established tradition in Canada as witnessed by the Cup symbolizing football supremacy in Canada, which was donated by His Excellency, the late Governor General Earl Grey in 1909 for that purpose;
Mr. Speaker, they claim in a peremptory fashion that football is a tradition. Although this may be the case, they try to turn it into a basic principle, which I feel is a mistake, for what does the word "tradition" mean and how can football be considered a really true Canadian tradition? Perhaps it is because I come from the province of Quebec, but I do not feel I could agree with this point. In my opinion, the tradition they are talking about here is the following: football provides the Prime Minister with a once a year opportunity to "kick the ball" and show himself in public in more or less garish outfits. This is what struck me especially, and if it is a tradition, I wonder if we could not do without it.

No one has ever been too concerned about it, to the extent where American professionalism has managed to take over, to all practical intents, a sport which in fact is our true national sport.
Mr. Speaker, by opposing hockey to football I want to prove that the preamble of the bill is misleading. It is not true that football is a truly Canadian sport. Back home in the riding of Champlain, I never see lads practicing that sport.

The proof of that is that there are nearly no professional football players who are Quebecers or French Canadians. I say so not to bring in nationalism but to contradict the minister. It is not true that it is a national sport nor that it interests all Canadians.
There is a sport whether it be in St. John's, Newfoundland, in Quebec City or elsewhere in the province of Quebec, in Ontario, in B.C. or even in the Northwest Territories in which all Canadians are interested. Sport belongs to everyone. There are no reserved rights to any sport. Even if we were somewhat hurt in our pride when we lost the world amateur hockey championships
Canadian Professional Football the fact still remains that we are proud that our national sport was born and grew in Canada, became a world sport, particularly appreciated in Europe where it has been developed to such an extent that today in the amateur branch Europeans are better than we are.
Mr. Speaker, if we wanted to enhance somewhat the prestige of Canada, if we wanted to preserve something worthwhile we should consider developing our national sport at home a bit like the Russians do, Mr. Speaker. We could follow their example.
It would be marvelous to have in Canada a Canadian national league of high amateur or semi-professional calibre in which all provinces would be represented and we would have the best prospects in junior hockey in this country. That would be a concrete and useful action for there is a lack in that area. If some legislation should really be passed in favour of sport and if it is desired to implement the principles indicated in the preamble of Bill C-22, I think, Mr. Speaker, that it has been a failure. There should be some motivation for Canadians to preserve their really national sport, in order to help not only hockey as such but all the youth of Canada to have the ambition one day of playing in a truly Canadian league made up of the best players. At any rate, I do not know what has bitten the minister for putting forward this legislation when the situation is growing more critical and that we are facing all kinds of problems. Mr. Speaker, the contribution by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) may be the most significant that has yet been given in the context of this debate. Perhaps it is appropriate for me to begin my remarks in a debate like this by stating some basic propositions. These propositions may be seen as fundamental goals and objectives. It may be they will meet with general agreement in this House and across the country.
The first proposition is that the Canadian game of football is unique. It is different in form from its American counterpart. It is probably preferred by the majority of Canadians.
The second proposition is that the Canadian Football League, as the only professional league in which Canadian football is played, should be given an opportunity to continue as an entertainment and sporting vehicle for Canadian fans. It should also provide professional career opportunities for aspiring young Canadians.
The third proposition is that the Grey Cup Game, being about the closest thing Canada has to a national festival, should be preserved as a vehicle for bringing together Canadians from east and west in a sporting context.
I am sure the government will agree with those three propositions. Indeed, in the preamble to the bill before us, I detect a certain sympathy for them. Where I quarrel with the government is in the actual means it has employed to achieve the goals and objectives I have stated, and perhaps others which I have not stated.
I would first observe that the government appears to have been putting its head in the sand by refusing to recognize what is happening in professional sports in North America. I need only make a passing reference to pro hockey expansion, pro baseball expansion, pro basket-

ball expansion, pro lacrosse expansion and pro tennis expansion to indicate generally what I mean. Consumer demand for professional sports is increasing, precipitated largely by television coverage. Professional opportunities for good young players, regardless of their country of origin, have almost doubled in a very short period of time.
What is happening with football? We all remember the American Football League, a bunch of upstarts who could not hold a candle to the Canadian Football League, let alone the National Football League. Where is the AFL now? It has emerged as part of a giant major league operation in the country to the south of us.
Through evolution, we now see a third major league on its way up. The important thing for Canadians to remember is that the price is going up. It is just like oil. The supply of players for the most part has remained constant, but the demand has been increasing. What happens when demand increases and supply remains about the same? The price goes up. Regardless of what the government of Canada does, regardless of what this parliament does and regardless of what legislation is actually enacted as the law of this country, there is going to be a significant impact on Canadian professional football by economic events I have described in the North American context.
The salaries of players are going up regardless of whether we have legislation. The cost of equipment and stadia, is going up regardless of whether we have legislation. There is going to be more competition in television from the new U.S, leagues regardless of what happens to this bill. Most important, there is going to be some raiding of the Canadian Football League. There is going to be a significant amount of raiding if this bill goes through.
What about this purely Canadian league which the government is attempting to insulate from international competition? This bill does not say anything about salaries. There is nothing here about the cost of equipment and stad to our Canadian cities. There is nothing about television competition from the leagues to the south. Indeed, the government owned CBC is apparently going to continue to nurture Canadian interest in the American game by televising NFL games on Sunday. Most important, there is nothing in this bill about the raiding that will go on.
One of the significant practical implications of events to date leading up to the introduction of this bill has been the guarantees given by Canadian owners of the Toronto franchise in the World Football League. There have been guarantees related to equalization and no television competition, which I will describe and go into in a moment. I think the most important guarantee was with regard to raiding. I wish to quote from a document which was presented to all members of parliament and the government by the owners of the Northmen. I quote:
If we remain in Canada, we are prepared to urge upon our associates the adoption of the same policy against the signing of "futures".
That is a policy between the National Football League and the CFL.
Since our associates are anxious to have a team located in Toronto we would expect them to accept this suggestion. If the signing of "futures" is permitted to continue, we would expect that fully 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the present name players in the Canadian Football League will not be playing in the CFL next year.

If the Northmen are allowed to play in Toronto, there will be an attempt to avoid the signing of CFL players into that new league. That is a league promise, not a Northmen promise. It is not a Northmen threat of any sort, but a fact of life of the WFL. It is a statement and a guarantee that we have every indication they will be prepared to live up to.
I have given the international and the North American background to professional football and professional sports generally. Strangely enough, when this government is dealing with a matter such as inflation, it is only too willing to blame international factors as being the cause of the problem. They throw up their collective arms and say "We can do nothing about it; it is international in nature." However, when the matter comes down to a really important aspect such as the game of football, what happens to the international aspect of it? It is ignored. We have "head-in-the-sand", restrictive prohibitive legislation as the immediate solution. As virtually every speaker from this side of the House has said, the government has got its priorities mixed up.
To put it in a nutshell, my fear is that this legislation may do more harm to the Canadian game of football, the Canadian Football League and the Grey Cup than would be the case if the government had kept its nose out of the whole area of professional sport. Canadian football is a good game. I happen to like it. I watch a lot of it over television and I attend the occasional Argo game. In the words of Russ Jackson, we in Toronto have to look at some of the practical and economic facts of life. Russ Jackson, who is no stranger to Canadian football, said "Toronto is a strong enough football town to support both the Argonauts and the World Football League."
I hope the CFL will survive. I hope the Argos will survive and prosper within that league. Indeed, they may even win the Grey Cup some day. However, with a potential market of some two to three million people in this country, the Argos playing to a packed house and many thousands of Torontonians unable to get access to the stadium to watch that fabulous team, the addition of another professional team should not warrant the kind of negative concern that emanated from the government benches and which is manifested in the bill before us today.
If this bill passes, what will happen to the Northmen? What will the impact be on the CFL? We saw in this morning's paper that the Northmen may go to Seattle. I ask all hon. members from southern British Columbia what impact this will have on the Vancouver Lions. Television rights will be involved. Northmen games will be beamed right into Vancouver. I suggest that from time to time a busload of people will go to Seattle to watch the games.
Alternatively, the Northmen may go to Buffalo. What would happen in that case? I am told that some 5,000 Torontonians presently journey to Buffalo every Sunday to watch the Buffalo Bills. It would not be difficult for the owners of the Northmen to lay on extra buses, a few extra trainloads, and take thousands and thousands of Torontonians down to Buffalo, or for the CTV network or for
Canadian Professional Football the major radio stations in the Toronto area to continue to broadcast those games because of the factor of Canadian ownership of the team which enables it to qualify as having Canadian content. What will happen to the Argos in this context, particularly when there is this real possibility that the World Football League will be taking the most important Canadian players out of our country and into their league? I think we can see the direction in which the whole shooting match can go.
I have put the argument in favour of not passing legislation with the intent to preserve Canadian football and the Canadian Football League and the Grey Cup. But let us look at the other side of the question, since we ought to be realistic and honest in a debate such as this. What if the Canadian Football League is too weak to face the competition in the marketplace? Despite the recent pleas of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) in the debate on the competition bill for more competition in professional sport, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) insists on proceeding with this protectionist measure. Let us take a hard look at what he is protecting. On Thursday, the minister told us why he feels the CFL is more Canadian than apple pie. I quote:
The only completely Canadian-controlled professional sports league in Canada is the CFL.
Take a look at the Canadian Football League. Seventy-five per cent of all revenue generated by that league is paid into the hands of Americans. Virtually every quarterback, coach and general manager in the Canadian Football League is an American, or was an American when he entered the league. The star players, the ones the fans pay to see, are Americans for the most part. Finally, an increasing number of the Canadians who do make the big time, maybe one third, who are good enough to become well paid stars in the CFL, receive their early training at United States colleges, playing the American game. This is the league we are preserving as a Canadian league.
The truth is that the CFL cannot be effectively isolated from the North American marketplace. It never has been and the government may be hypocritical that it can be, now. If the government is really serious about Canadianiz-ing the CFL it would have carried its legislation much further. Let me suggests some additional clauses it might have inserted. It would have increased the minimum Canadian content in terms of players to 75 per cent. Or why not carry it right through to 100 per cent so that all the players would be Canadians-no imports at all would be allowed.
Allow me to suggest a further amendment. The minister and the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) have made noises about new Canadian teams entering the CFL-teams from London, Ontario, and Halifax-Dart-mouth were suggested. Why not tell the CFL to put its money where its mouth is? Why not make provision in this bill whereby any Canadian city of reasonable size which can provide a stadium with 20,000 seats would be entitled as of right to a CFL franchise? This would be the kind of quid pro quo the government should demand for giving to the CFL the protection it is giving the league in the bill before us.
But looking at the issue seriously, we all know that the CFL is really not all that Canadian. There are only limited

opportunities open to aspiring young Canadian footballers to make it into the big time in the league. The big salaries will still go to the Americans, as they always have. I think this is bad. Many of our young hockey players have found a whole new world of possibilities opened up to them and I, for one, would not wish to support legislation which might have the effect of restricting that prospect for them.
What has the Minister of National Health and Welfare done beside issue an occasional threat and, of course, issue the bill we are now considering? Perhaps he could tell us at some time during the debate, if not in committee, what communication he has had with the executives of the National Football League, or with its president. After all, that is the league which is the big threat, the league which may well go into Montreal. In many respects, the Toronto Northmen and the WFL are being made scapegoats. Has he attempted to extract from the president of the NFL an undertaking not to come into Canada because doing so would run contrary to government policy? I have seen no evidence of any such communications, and I would be delighted to hear the minister or his parliamentary secretary outline to us the form and nature of any communications with the National Football League.
I would also ask the minister what communication has taken place with the Mayor of Montreal. The Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) might care to tell us what communication he has had with the Mayor of Montreal in connection with the new stadium which is to be financed at least in part through a scheme for the sale of coins and postage stamps which is federally sponsored. It may be the Mayor has since seen the light. It may be that he will be willing to compromise. I should like to see some evidence that an attempt has been made to communicate with the Mayor of Montreal. I know an

attempt has been made to communicate with the Mayor of Toronto and with the Metropolitan Chairman in that city.
But what we do know, on the minister's own admission, is that he did not communicate with the owners of the Toronto Northmen prior to his speech in Regina on February 21, notwithstanding the fact that the establishment of that WFL franchise in Toronto was announced six months earlier, in August 1973. The news appeared, of course, in all the daily newspapers and was broadcast throughout the country. It was well known not only to sports fans but, I suggest, to the government. My feeling is that if the minister were willing to communicate a little more readily he would need to legislate a little less. To his credit, the minister conducted two meetings with the owners of the Northmen in mid-March, after he had let the axe fall in Regina on February 21.
But despite all the guarantees the owners of the Northmen were willing to provide, a guarantee to make up the loss of equalization, a guarantee not to expand the league into any other city, a guarantee of no competing national television coverage, and a guarantee that there would be no raiding, the minister on April 10 brought forth a bill which is restrictive and retroactive, virtually cutting off all communication. In other words, the minister threw down the gauntlet and they are prepared to do battle. I find that course of behaviour a little strange, particularly in view of the comments made by the hon. member for York West who followed the minister as the only other government speaker who has had the nerve to enter this debate.
I quote from that hon. member for York West, who I am delighted to see in his place, who gave his version of how communications were operating between the government and those to be affected by this bill:
I remind my hon. friends opposite that the government was forced to legislate, after having made its policy eminently clear through the former minister of national health and welfare some 17 months ago, and reaffirmed by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) when he took over that portfolio. The government was forced into legislating, and now this bill is before the House.
I ask hon. members and all the people in the Toronto area, who forced the government? Where is this great body of opinion that required the government to come forward in response to this widespread demand? The government was forced by whom? I suggest that the hon. member for York West may have his political blinkers on because he said later in his speech:
I am confident that the overwhelming majority of Torontonians, given a chance to understand this issue, are going to support the government-
The hon. member for York West has put his neck on the line. Let him come out and speak in Toronto on this very issue.

While plans to expand the Toronto stadium may eventually contribute to alleviating this situation, any such expansion may take some time and still might not meet the demand for seats. Accordingly, an undertaking has been given by the owner of the Argonauts that on an experimental basis, and beginning this season, the television blackout would be lifted when it was established in advance that the game would be a sellout. The minister is fully aware that such a decision cannot be made by any individual CFL club without the approval of other clubs in the League, but the Commissioner of the CFL has undertaken to put such a proposition before the other CFL club members, and to encourage its acceptance.
That is the sop to the people of Toronto, and it might be a meaningful sop if the government could do what it has promised. What the minister forgot to tell the people of Toronto was that there had to be some other approvals which might not be forthcoming. It is one thing for him not to tell the public of Canada that there had to be approval of the Canadian National Exhibition, which actually owns the stadium and has certain contractual rights,
Canadian Professional Football of which the minister was well aware as he is a lawyer. He is well aware, too, that the Argonaut owner, just because of a unilateral representation from the federal government, cannot back out of his contracts. Indeed, I believe the commissioner of the CFL, or the Argonaut president, Lou Hayman, said on the weekend that in addition to the approval of other teams in the CFL, they will have to honour their contract with the CNE, because that contract gives the CNE the right to approval as well.
As if that were not enough, there is this other indication that the owners of the Argonauts have certain contractual obligations with the radio station. In this case it happens to be a rather substantial contractual obligation with Radio Station CFTR, which entered into the agreement before all this matter arose, with certainly a large amount of money involved, I think in the area of $125,000 the first year, for exclusive rights to broadcast Argonaut home games. If there is going to be no television blackout when the stadium is sold out, the radio rights are not going to be worth nearly as much as they would otherwise be, as people will watch the television as opposed to listening to the radio when they cannot go to see the game, and the owner of the Argonauts knew of this contractual right when he gave his undertaking to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I am not suggesting that the minister knew of this contractual right, but again I am putting before the House the fact that the minister is a lawyer and now has become somewhat of an expert, I hope, on how professional football teams operate. He should have realized he was holding out a false promise, which may in fact be the cruelest hoax on the people of Toronto, to suggest that TV blackouts will be lifted. The minister does not have any guarantee, and neither does Mr. Gaudaur, that there will be an agreement forthcoming from every CFL team, and indeed there may be some indication to the contrary. I am happy to sit back and watch what happens in that regard, but for the moment I think it is cruel, and it may be somewhat deceitful, for the government to hold out to the people of Toronto the hope that next fall they will see Argonaut home games on television.
Mention has already been made by two hon. members, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) about the problem of the constitutional validity of Bill C-22. This is a complex matter and perhaps one that is better argued in the courts than in the House of Commons. After all, though, the House of Commons is regarded by many as the highest court of the land and I think it would be inappropriate if not irresponsible if opposition members were to let a bill of this nature pass without commenting on the constitutional problem which appears so obvious on the face of the legislation. I refer specifically to this most restrictive clause of the bill, Clause 6 which reads:
Subject to this section, no person owning, operating or managing a football team within a foreign league shall require or permit that team to play football in Canada.
Subclause (2) reads:
Subject to this section, no person shall play football within Canada as a member of, or as a player on, a football team within a foreign league.

April 22, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
Subclause (3) merely goes on to provide an exception in the case of exhibition games. How can the federal government justify the constitutional validity of this particular clause? Prior to the introduction of the bill we heard reference to trade and commerce powers, and we have also heard reference from time to time to the powers of the government in respect of immigration in the British North America Act. We have heard reference during this debate to the emergency power, the so-called peace, order and good government power of the federal parliament. Of course, the federal government has undisputed jurisdiction over criminal law and procedure under Section 127 of the British North America Act.
I think at the very least it should be incumbent on the minister, when he knew there were problems in respect of the constitutional validity of this bill, to explain the justification upon which the government was prepared to rely to support the validity of this bill. I say to the minister and to his parliamentary secretary that these may be the type of questions opposition members will want to put to the minister and his officials when the bill goes to the committee in the very near future. It will go to the committee very shortly provided it survives the vote, which is questionable. There is a question in my mind concerning how one can support legislation which focuses on the playing of a game within a province. This legislation does not relate to a commercial process or interprovincial or international boundaries. It contains a criminal prohibition relating to the playing of a game. The criminal sanction is invoked when the player in that game or the person who happens to be owner, manager or coach is with a team belonging to a foreign league. In other words, the crime is belonging to a foreign league and playing the game of football.
It has already been pointed out by several speakers that legislation relating to the playing of a game, traditionally at least, has fallen within the purview of the province. About the only legislation to my knowledge that has been supported as valid federal legislation related to the playing of games relates to pinball machines. This type of legislation, which is included in the Criminal Code, has been sustained on the ground that it has an element of immorality attached to it. In other words, there is something morally wrong or mischievous about playing this machine. Perhaps it leads to an unreasonable propensity to gamble. I challenge the government to prove what moral aspect exists in respect of playing football in Canada merely because the people involved happen to be part of a foreign league.
I predict what will happen is that this legislation will be in trouble when it goes before the courts. I say in all seriousness that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who apparently drafted this bill has the statutory obligation to check the provisions of this bill to determine whether or not they are constitutional in respect of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The phrase in the Canadian Bill of Rights to which I refer is "equality before the law". There are certain protections in respect of equality before the law and against discrimination on account of national origin which exist in the Canadian Bill of Rights.

In the first instance, I think the Minister of Justice has a statutory obligation to come before the House and say that he has checked the bill and that it is constitutional in that it complies with the Canadian Bill of Rights. As the government well knows, it is open to any person affected by legislation, including the government itself, to test the bill to determine its consistency or inconsistency with the Canadian Bill of Rights. I repeat that I think the government has the duty to come forward and say that the law officers have looked at this legislation and that in their opinion it is proper. This has not taken place.
In conclusion I wish to ask some questions about the implications of this bill in relation to things other than professional football. I might ask what are the implications of this legislation in respect of other sports. We have heard mention of hockey, baseball and soccer. I am sure the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) would be interested in this game and the implications of this bill related to professional soccer as played in Toronto. Let us consider other forms of entertainment and culture such as ballet, music, opera, theatre and painting. What are the implications of restrictive legislation of this sort in that area? I find this a little frightening. I hesitate to use the term but I think we must consider this. There has been a great national debate about football.
One of the most prominent figures in this debate now is the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Some sports columnists have suggested that this legislation is devious.
I think that is unfair. Some suggest it has been introduced for partisan political purposes. I think that is unfair. Indeed, I think if the Minister of National Health and Welfare thought about it and considered the political winds of change, he would realize that this bill may not bring any political advantage. I think the minister was serious in bringing forward the bill. If I can be charitable,
I believe he was ill advised perhaps in doing so. That is the way I would characterize his attempt to enact this legislation, and apparently it is too late at least in his opinion to withdraw this bill.
Today during the question period the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said we should end this debate and move on to other things. He agreed with the comments of questioners from this side of the House and said that the simplest way to move on to other things would be for those on this side of the House to stop talking. I think I can speak for most of us on this side of the House when I say that we will end this debate immediately if the government will do the one thing it should do under the circumstances, and that is to withdraw the bill.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I say I regret that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has seen fit to involve himself in professional sports. We are all aware of the fact that hon. members of this House welcome the idea of the physical fitness and amateur sports assistance made available by the government. I think it is more fact than rumour that the NHL headquarters will be moving out of Montreal when Mr. Campbell completes his term of office. There goes the national aspect of the Canadian game! Will the minister be prepared to introduce legislation to compel the National Hockey League-we have only three teams left in this country-to keep its headquarters in this country where it
April 22, 1974

belongs. We might look at the preamble to the bill. It begins this way:
Whereas football has an established tradition in Canada as witnessed by the Cup symbolizing football supremacy in Canada, which was donated by His Excellency, the late Governor General Earl Grey in 1909 for that purpose;
That is absolutely false and incorrect. I am under the impression that probably the minister received some pretty bad advice from Senator Keith Davey whose tenure of office as Commissioner of the football league did not see him through one season. I think the failure of Senator Davey has a lot to do with the minister being poorly advised.
Now we come to the definitions in the bill and we find the following one:
"football" means Canadian football and American football but does not include soccer or rugby;
How has the minister gone so wrong? In the first place, let me point out that Governor General Earl Grey donated the Grey Cup for rugby football, not professional football. In those days rugby football was played as an amateur sport. On what has the minister based himself? The minister referred to all the things that have been said in favour of the action proposed by the government in this bill. He quoted various authorities. He quoted the players' associations, and he came up with the name of George Reed who is an American. I want it completely understood here that I am not criticizing George Reed as a football player. His contribution to the game in Canada has been outstanding. No man has ever established the records that he has, nor do I think anyone will for a long time approach the record that this man has established. He has meant much to the game in Canada and to the team for which he plays. George Reed stands alone in this particular sport. He has been symbolic of the best there is. However, when the minister, speaking about protecting the Canadian Football League, quotes an American player, I think he is straying far from the intention of his legislation.
Now let us speak for a minute about the game itself and the importance of competition. I think, personally, that the establishment of more teams in Canada is good. It will certainly provide greater opportunities for a greater number of Canadians to participate in the sport in view of the fact that a certain number of them will have to fill up the rosters. It is a possibility that the opening up of opportunities and the establishment of more teams will cause the deterioration of the game. But that does not mean a thing. It is competition that makes the game, no matter what type of game is being played.
I can say without fear of contradiction that the worst game of hockey I ever watched was between the Chicago Black Hawks and the Toronto Maple Leafs. I watched the best players and at the same time I watched the worst game. It is the competition that counts. Horseracing fans in this country will know that a race run in two-eighteen or two-twenty can be just as exciting as one run in two flat because of the competition. It is what is happening at the end of the game which makes the game itself come alive-it is competition.
Canadian Professional Football
I am also somewhat disturbed about the geography brought in here. First we talk about Vancouver, and then we come all the way down to Montreal. I always understood that the country stretched from Victoria to St. John's, Newfoundland.
Hear, hear!

The bill refers to the national aspects of the game. There is nobody more fond of watching American football than I am. Even if I have to be fed my supper watching television-we are not too sophisticated down in Nova Scotia and we still have supper in the evening-I will not miss any of the game. If necessary, I will stay up after midnight watching the games from the west coast which we do not get until after midnight in the east. I follow the game; I like the game; I like to watch Sunday afternoon games. I will not support anything here that will deprive me or anyone else in eastern Canada of the opportunity of watching American football games on Sunday afternoons. While in Ottawa I like nothing better than to watch American college teams perform. I think that they perform more excitingly than any of the professional leagues. They may lack a good deal in finesse but they make up for it in desperation, and to me that makes for a better game.
When we talk about the geography of the country and the national aspect of this game we overlook the fact that eastern Canada does not stop in Montreal and that western Canada does not stop in Vancouver. Reference is made to the financial aspect and to what the league is doing for the teams in the amateur ranks in Canada. Let me point out that what they are doing is purely in their own interests. If there is any subsidy given by professional sports in this country to give an opportunity to the younger men in the sport, it is done with the sole purpose of pulling these young men into the professional league and the professional team. It is self-serving and the assistance is not provided under physical fitness and amateur sports legislation which is something worthwhile. Believe me, professional sport is a business and any financial assistance they give to any minor league team is given with one purpose in mind, to strengthen their own position.
Earlier I spoke about the donation of the Grey Cup by the late Governor General Earl Grey in 1909 and the fact that the definition in the bill states that football is Canadian football and American football, but does not include soccer or rugby. This is absolutely wrong. I still say, and if I were still involved I would make the claim, that any rugby team in Canada that can prove itself superior can lay claim to the Grey Cup which was originally intended as a rugby award. Somehow or other Canadian football got past the Rules and the Grey Cup was awarded to professionals playing Canadian football, but it was never donated for any such purpose in the first place.
Let me tell you something about the history of the game. Originally the first game was rugby. When we talk about the international game we know that rugby football has a far greater appeal on the world scene than either the Canadian or American football games. I think we would all admit that probably soccer is the greatest of the international games, the game which is played in most coun-

April 22, 1974
Canadian Professional Football
tries. Perhaps now that the European countries have taken up hockey, we could consider hockey to be close to the top also. I would say that basketball also has gone up a long way in popularity. It was the Canadians who invented basketball and the Americans took it over.
However, speaking of international games, rugby must be up at the top in popularity. The French team is one of the leading teams in Europe. We have all heard of the New Zealand All Blacks-a famous name for years. They are playing Wales, Scotland and Ireland. They have played all over Europe, in Canada and the United States as well. A few moments ago someone mentioned that soccer is becoming professionalized. Indeed, Toronto has a soccer team in the professional league. Why is there so much emphasis on the Canadian-American football game? What I will say now may be a denial of what I originally said. I enjoy watching the game, but I have no choice. However, I will try to give members of the House an opportunity to see a game later this week. I have arranged to have a film shown here and I invite everybody here to look at that film. It will show a game played between the New Zealand All Blacks and the Barbarians. You will see 80 minutes of sustained action. This is the game for which the Grey Cup was originally intended.
I say that with proper promotion amateur football can take over in this country. You will be watching a football spectacle that will make your Grey Cup games look like child's play in comparison. Why do I say that? Because in this game a player goes on the field for 80 minutes. What do our professionals do? Probably they play for 15, 17 or 18 minutes, and between the shuffle that goes on between the bench, the field and the delays, the game lasts three hours. I intend to watch 60 minutes of football and it takes me three hours to do it. With amateur sports you get 80 minutes of football all wrapped up in an hour and a half or an hour and 40 minutes. This is sustained action. You will see the pro coming off the bench; he will run down the field 75 yards, either complete the run or miss a pass and the coach will give him a breather. This is professional sport. There is sustained action for 80 minutes; there is continuous football, such as the Grey Cup was originally intended for.
As we delve into the history of the game, what do we find? The game which was played by the American ivy league by Rutgers, Brown, Princeton, Harvard, Yale and other similar colleges, is based on English football. We call it English football in my area; actually we should refer to it as rugby football. How did the American game develop to its present form? According to history, and I am talking off the top of my head but have read the facts, Harvard built an enormous stadium, only to find that not enough room was left for the playing surface. They had to narrow the field, therefore, cut down the length and begin innovating with regards to the rules. That is how we developed the forward pass, which is supposed to make the game so glamorous. I sound as if I hate the game, but I do not. I like to watch sports events and will continue to watch in future. I hope I will not be denied the opportunity by the ridiculous measure the minister has brought before the House.

The game as we know it developed from rugby football, and began because some people decided to reduce the dimensions of the playing field and make innovations in the rules. The minister has stepped into the area of professional sport. What will this do for the development of football in Canada? I don't know. I think he is playing a dangerous game. I have learned that the Senate of the United States is considering measures of retaliation whereby they will restrict the number of Canadian hockey players who may play on American NHL teams. Perhaps this will turn some players loose. They could come back to Canada and be absorbed in an NHL team, go to Winnipeg, or possibly Ottawa. We all know what happened to the last professional hockey team that tried to establish itself in Ottawa. I think we are playing a dangerous game when we tamper with professional sports. We are becoming involved with business. The minister may be restricting the entry of Americans to our game, but he is running the risk of having our hockey players excluded from the United States.
That brings me to another point. Look at what happened to the Canadian intercollegiate basketball finalists not long ago. What went on was shameful. There is a small university in Nova Scotia which has a tremendous record in intercollegiate sports. It was finalist two years in a row in intercollegiate hockey, winner of the 1973 Canadian football championship and won last year the Canadian basketball championship. Again this year, the team was a finalist in the Canadian basketball championship.
When that team went to play, what happened? There were three American players in the line-up and what anthem did the band play? Did it play O Canada? Not on your life. It was decided, because there were three Americans on the team, that the band would play the Star Spangled Banner. Is this the way to treat a maritime university because there are three American players on the team; is that any reason to play the American national anthem rather than the Canadian national anthem? Is this the kind of treatment we can expect for people east of Montreal.
The preamble to the bill is based on facts which are not correct. Look at the history of the game. The Grey Cup trophy was never intended to be a trophy for professional sports. It was intended for the best team playing rugby football, and rugby football developed into American style football through an accident. If you want to see real football, you should see a film which is available from Toronto. You will see, 80 minutes of sustained action. At the least you will see 45 minutes of action. You will see football as it should be played. You will not see players spending 20 or 25 minutes in a huddle, or using up time in scrimmages. The game is fast moving. Let me tell you, if professional athletes had to perform in the way these players perform for 80 minutes, they would be exhausted. You will be most impressed with these players. I urge members to see the film.
Returning to my original theme, what will the minister do if the Americans decide to retaliate and exclude NHL players from participating with American teams, or limit the number of Canadian hockey players who may play with an American team. As I said, there is a bill to that effect coming before the American Senate. It requires a
April 22, 1974

certain percentage of players on American teams to be Americans. If that bill is enacted into law, many would-be Canadian hockey players will be denied opportunities because of the geographic area from which they come. What about the subsidy, in a manner of speaking, which is to be provided by the professional football league in Canada. Will it apply to Cape Breton, to Nova Scotia, to P.E.I., to Newfoundland and to other areas?
I have not listened to the debate up to now. However, as soon as I looked at the first paragraph of the preamble to the bill, I knew the minister was wrong. In addition, the definition section of the bill says, football means Canadian football and American football but does not include soccer or rugby. That is entirely wrong and flies in the face of why Governor General Grey in 1909 presented the trophy. That section and that preamble constitute an absolute denial of the original reason for presenting the Grey Cup.
In making these remarks I do not intend to involve myself in the financial aspects or the TV coverage aspect of Canadian or American football. Again, I say on my own behalf and on behalf of lots of people in the maritime provinces that, if this bill becomes law, we may be denied the opportunity to watch games, as we have done in the past.
The physical fitness and amateur sport legislation is well worth supporting. I think it is supported by members on both sides of the House. I have, at times, criticized what is going on within the responsible department; I have also criticized groups who have come forward for financial assistance under the act. For instance, I do not consider chess to be a game which deserves financial support from the physical fitness and amateur sport branch of the department. How much physical fitness are you developing when you sit down to play a game of chess? I think it should be directed into those sports which are strictly amateur in nature. Later, there is nothing to prevent an amateur from turning professional, of course. The preamble to this bill is absolutely wrong, absolutely false and inaccurate. You can apply any adjective you wish, but it does not belong in the legislation nor does discrimination, as I outlined, in the definition.
I hope the minister will stop heeding the bad advice he is getting, which I assume comes from the short-lived commissioner, Senator Davey. I could be wrong but there is no doubt in my mind that this matter has been brought before parliament strictly on a political basis. It is strictly political. What they hope to gain I do not know, but I do not see how restricting competition can do any good.
If Americans begin to retaliate there will not be much left and in the end we will probably get back to what was originally intended-that is, playing a game of football for 80 minutes of sustained play rather than 17 or 18 minutes per game for the professionals who have to stop for a breather after a 70 yard dash. In rugby union football you run 75 yards and get knocked on your butt. Then, you have to pick yourself up and run another 75 yards. There is none of this pampering.
This is a dangerous area in which the minister has moved. If he is going to be consistent in his approach to
Point of Order
professional sports, I think he had better amend his bill to provide that the Montreal Expos baseball team should have a percentage of Canadian players. If the legislation applies to professional football, why not apply it to baseball and make the Expos use a percentage of Canadian players in their lineups. What would that do to professional baseball in the Montreal area? We all know it would absolutely chase it out of Montreal.
I do not think the minister has been properly advised on bringing in this bill. In fact, he has been poorly advised on the restrictive type of legislation which will only be detrimental to other professional sports throughout the country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS-PUBLIC BILLS   IDENTIFICATION OF CRIMINALS ACT AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT PUBLICATION AND DESTROY RESULTS OF IDENTIFICATION PROCESS UPON ACQUITTAL

speechtext:
Mr. tJ.-J. Blais (Nipissing) moved: That Bill C-220, An Act to amend the Identification of Criminals Act, be read for the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to submit my first bill since I have been elected to this Chamber. I have many times had the opportunity to adopt a negative attitude towards bill submitted by other colleagues who are, in fact, here in the House. I was very sorry to see their bills dropped at the bottom of the list, because we did not have enough time to discuss them. I hope that this tradition will not be followed this time and that we will have the opportunity to see the bill I am now submitting to the House debated in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that, of course, the essential amendments I am now proposing to the bill regarding the identification of criminals be adopted, since I think they are vital. So that we may discuss this bill in committee, my participation will be very short, but clear and accurate.
The bill that I suggest be amended concerns the Identification of Criminals Act. This act allows the police, investigators, Crown officers, even before an individual is convicted, to prepare and compile a file for identification purposes in relation with this individual. However, this may present some difficulty. As everyone knows, there is a fundamental principle in our criminal justice system according to which every accused must be presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.
On various occasions, we have attempted to change this principle a little, but without success. However, I believe that the Identification of Criminals Act is in direct opposition to this principle which is part of the English common law and which we have always tried to sanctify, indeed, to perpetuate.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
One has to read section one very carefully. It speaks of the identification of criminals. Therefore, it speaks of the identification of people who, under our law are deemed to be criminals. Section 2 reads:
Any person in lawful custody, charged with, or under conviction of an indictable offence, or who has been apprehended under the Extradition Act or the Fugitive Offenders Act, may be subjected, by or under the direction of those in whose custody he is, to the measurements, processes and operations practised under the system for the identification of criminals commonly known as the Bertillon Signaletic System, or to any measurements, processes or operations sanctioned by the Governor in Council having the like object in view.
I stress the fact that those people who are subjected to this system of identification are those in lawful custody or charged under a criminal statute. Under this bill, there is no necessity that the person be convicted, be brought before a tribunal, be arraigned or indicted. There is simply the need for that person to be lawfully arrested or charged. Whether that charge is proceeded with is of absolutely no merit.
The question is whether he has been charged and whether he is under lawful arrest. If those two criteria are met, the whole procedure of identification falls into place. That may not be absolutely detrimental to our whole system of criminal justice, but I draw Your Honour's attention to Section 3 which reads:
No one having the custody of any such person, and no one acting in his aid or under his direction, and no one concerned in such publication, incurs any liability, civil or criminal, for anything lawfully done under this Act.
Sections 2 and 3 permit the complete publication of any information obtained through this identification procedure. It permits the dissemination of that information at any time without any limitation, notwithstanding the fact that that particular person has never been produced before any court in this country and has never been convicted of any offence. Therein lies the big fault of the statute as it now exists, namely that individuals are subjected to identification although there has only been a charge levelled against them and that information is subject to publication.
This can be done in any way the constabulary sees fit. There is no remedy offered under civil or criminal justice. Although Section 3 limits this publication only to those engaged in the execution or administration of the law, that particular group can be very wide indeed. That publication could be very detrimental. In the course of its publication, it could well be that the information is obtained by the press, news media or other citizens who may well want to make use of it even before the individual appears before a tribunal or is convicted. I draw Your Honour's attention to the Canadian Bill of Rights.

Mr. Speaker, clause 2 reads as follows:
2. Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an Act of the Parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or feeedoms herein recognized and declared, and in particular, no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to ...

It is essential that this bill be passed because it orders the destruction of cards and other results of the identification process wherever anyone has been acquitted of the offence with which he was charged or discharged under the recent amendments to the Criminal Code.
In conclusion, perhaps in anticipation of an argument which might be presented, I simply want to state my rejection of that argument. It has been indicated to me that this information serves to identify criminals who, although they have not been convicted before a court of the country, are engaged in criminal activity. I suggest that the exception must be very rare. It does not outweigh the right of any Canadian citizen to be deemed innocent until proven guilty and the right of a Canadian citizen to not have published throughout the country an indication that he is under criminal charge. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your attention.

I want to say to him at the outset, in terms that I want to make as unqualified as I can, that I see nothing wrong with this bill.
I recognize the arguments that will be put forward. There will be those who in the name of assisting the police and so on will say that the right to publish mug shots and fingerprints should be retained without restriction. However, I think the essential point made in this bill, and in the speech of the hon. member for Nipissing, is valid, namely that until a person is proven guilty, he is innocent and that until he is charged and brought before a court, he should not be treated as though he were a criminal. I believe, therefore, that the hon. member for Nipissing has done a service in drafting and presenting this bill. Its purpose is clear. It contends that mug shots, fingerprints and other means of identification used with respect to persons who are in trouble with the law should not be published before that person is brought before a court; and if such a person is found to be not guilty, those various forms of identification should be destroyed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of showing a negative attitude to this bill. On the contrary, I see many good aspects in the bill. However, I believe it may be somewhat excessive.
Amendments should indeed be made to the Identification of Criminals Act, but the destruction of all criminal identification would be in my opinion a serious mistake, especially in the case of acquittals, because there is no proof that where persons are acquitted of an offence, they do no commit other offences later on.
The acquitted person is in fact often guilty. There is no doubt about it in anybody's mind. But because of circumstances surrounding the crime, because of the reasonable doubt benefitting the accused, and often through some jurors' incompetence, the accused is acquitted. But it is not proven that he never does commit other offences later on.
I remember a famous hearing in Quebec City, a few years ago. A certain individual had been accused of kidnap and murder, and was later on acquitted. I will not discuss how the jury came to such a decision but one thing I am sure of is that to destroy signaletic cards or identification papers concerning that individual would be a very serious mistake. Also, to destroy certain identification papers concerning, let us say certain present activists taking advantage of labour conflicts in Quebec for instance, would also be at this time a serious mistake.
However, in the case of juvenile delinquents who are brought before the social welfare courts, one could say perhaps that the judge shows a little more flexibility and since fingerprints and mugshots are not used in that case, I believe it is a good thing. As regards people accused for instance of having used drugs for non-medical purposes, they have the benefit of getting a suspended sentence. There again, I suggest identification papers for fingerprints should not be used. But I am thinking of the dope pushers who are declared not guilty and in such cases, I do not believe the fingerprints should be destroyed.
As a matter of fact, when we visited penitentiaries this year, we were told that 85 per cent of the prisoners were repeaters. Therefore, one could perhaps wonder how many of them were acquitted the first time. Again, I say one cannot be sure that an acquitted person will not commit a second or even a third offence. I would have suggestions to make about that. Again, there is much to be said for Bill 220, but over-indulgence is the weakness in some clauses. For instance, I think identification papers, fingerprints or mugshots should be destroyed, let us say after ten years, if

Identification of Criminals Act
the person did not commit any other crime. I also think that certain signaletic cards should be destroyed in the case of certain types of persons. I refer to young people who commit a crime through an excess due to their age, do not commit any more during a period of five or eight years. I think their cards should be destroyed.
I would also make a difference as regards persons acquitted in the case of a very serious offence or breach of the law. I refer here to those accused of sexual offences who are later acquitted.
I feel that those people should be set aside in a special category and, at the end of five or six years, their files could be destroyed.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I am not entirely against this bill but I would make certain amendments to it ensuring that the files of those who have been accused but not proven guilty are not completely destroyed.
