speechtext:
The House has probably devoted more attention in recent years to the subject of the convicted criminal than to the person whose case has not proceeded to a conviction. Several years ago we enacted the Criminal Records Act to provide a certain measure of relief in the case of people who had been convicted of offences, by way of directing that records shall, in a sense, be sealed after a certain period of time. Many of us who were involved with the progress of that bill, and the lengthy discussions which took place in the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, are concerned about the fact that so few of the provinces have done much to follow up this legislation and ensure that a person who has been convicted is not placed in an invidious position. A person who is convicted and has been pardoned ought to be able to say when he is answering the question: "Have you been convicted?" "No." Or perhaps we should insist that the question be framed so as to read: "Have you ever been convicted of a crime of which you have not been pardoned?"
People come to me in a difficult dilemma as to how to answer, as they have been convicted of a crime, served their sentence and have subsequently been pardoned and they are asked in some form of government process or questioning, usually not at the federal level,-and that is

where the problem comes in-"Have you ever been convicted of a crime?"
The clear intention of this legislation, which members of all parties of the House supported so strongly several years ago, was that persons should be able to answer "no" to that type of question, or at least have the assurance that the kind of question which could be asked would be very limited, indeed. There is a serious difficulty in the followup to the law by the provincial authorities. This parliament does not have complete legislative jurisdiction, as we all know, and there are many aspects of the problem which can be dealt with only by provincial law. I would suggest to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), who I understand does intend to bring in an amendment to this legislation during the present session, that he attempt to provide strong leadership to the provinces in order that the clear intention of parliament in this legislation can be observed.
I might also note along the same line that we have also provided that a person who is accused of an offence, and perhaps may even in a sense be guilty, may be given an absolute discharge before any conviction is registered. We have also done this to assist a person who either has committed an offence or, we might say, suspending judgment, may possibly have committed an offence. He is the kind of person we have been concerned about.
Referring to the explanatory note to this bill, we find pointed out there:
The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Identification of Criminals Act to provide that the results of the identification process e.g., mug shots, fingerprints may not be published unless and until the person in question has been convicted of the offence for which he was charged and subjected to the identification process. Similarly, provision is made for prohibiting the publication and for destroying the results of the identification process when the person has been acquitted.
I think in order to understand the change which the hon. member is purporting to make through this bill we ought to look at the legislation which is being amended and which, incidentally, happens to be one of the shortest pieces of legislation on the federal statute books. The full title is "An Act respecting the identification of criminals", but is more often cited as the Identification of Criminals Act. Since this is such a short act, I should like to read it in its entirety to the House.

I think the hon. member should allow me to make my own speech, Mr. Speaker, and I would note that he has taken up some time with his interjection. The second section of this legislation reads as follows:
Any person in lawful custody, charged with, or under conviction of an indictable offence, or who has been apprehended under the Extradition Act or the Fugitive Offenders Act, may be subjected, by or under the direction of those in whose custody he is, to the measurements, processes and operations practised under the system for the identification of criminals commonly known as the Bertillon Signaletic System, or to any measurements, processes or operations sanctioned by the Governor in Council having the like object in view.
(2)	Such force may be used as is necessary to the effectual carrying out and application of such measurements, processes and operations.
(3)	The signaletic cards and other results thereof may be published for the purpose of affording information to officers and others engaged in the execution or administration of the law.
April 22, 1974

It is this publication of fingerprints, etc., which the hon. member wishes to bring dramatically to our attention today. He has illustrated for us that we have to consider the provisions I have just read also in connection with Section 3 of the same Identification of Criminals Act, which I shall again just draw to the attention of the House as follows:
No one having the custody of any such person, and no one acting in his aid or under his direction, and no one concerned in such publication incurs any liability, civil or criminal, for anything lawfully done under this Act.
This Section 3 is a very broad exculpatory section which gives very complete, probably total, protection to all those who may act under Section 2 of the legislation and, therefore, is the kind of protection which the law should give only very cautiously.
As I understand the contention of the hon. member who proposes this legislation, he thinks we have not in the past in passing this legislation acted with sufficient care, and that the net covering what may be done, and what may be protected from potential lawsuit, has been cast far too wide. He proposes to remedy that by Bill C-220 which is before us for discussion this afternoon.
The actual changes the hon. member would make in the legislation, looking at the text of his Bill C-220, would be to change subsection 2(3) to the following:
Where the person who has been subjected to the measurements, processes and operations under subsection (1)
(a)	has been convicted of the offence with which he was charged,
(b)	has been ordered to be surrendered or returned pursuant to the
provisions of the Extradition Act or the Fugitive Offenders Act as the
case may be, or
(c)	has escaped lawful custody,
the signaletic cards and other results thereof may be published for the purpose of affording information to officers and others engaged in the execution or administration of the law.
His subsection (4) would be as follows:
Where the person who has been subjected to the measurements, processes and operations under subsection (1) has been acquitted of the offence with which he has been charged, or has been discharged pursuant to the provisions of the Extradition Act or the Fugitive Offenders Act as the case may be, the court shall prohibit the publication and order the destruction of the signaletic cards and other results of the identification process.
I share some of the doubts that have been expressed about this bill by the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), and I think perhaps the hon. member goes too far in what he proposes to do. As I understand the effect of his bill, and I trust I am reading this correctly, he would prohibit not only the giving of information in the public forum but would also prohibit the giving of it even in the internal forum of police work. The word that is used here in this section is "publish" and we normally think about this as publishing abroad, that is at large to the world. However, as we know from the traditional defamation action, publication can have a much more limited meaning than that. Even the contemporary connotation of "publish" in the written form in the newspaper or the monograph is not at all the only meaning of the word "publish". The word "publish" can be used even in respect of the transmission of an idea to a single person.
I recall that one committee of which I was a member decided for that reason that the word "publish" was not a
Identification of Criminals Act very good word to use. This was the committee on hate propaganda which reported to the federal government in 1965. This led, of course, to the amendment to the Criminal Code dealing with the subject of hate propaganda. This committee in its deliberations thought that the word "communication" would be a more precise word in the context of what was in question there, because its meaning clearly went further in the direction of providing for a situation which the word "publish" is not normally presumed to include in our normal conversation, though it is actually included in the legal and technical dictionary meaning.
So, I think the effect of the bill which my hon. friend is proposing would actually be to prohibit internal communication. How can our police forces possibly do their work adequately if they are unable to transmit information to other police forces?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not very kindly inclined towards criminals and I may not perhaps have cultivated the virtue of charity as much as my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but when I deal with criminals I am much more concerned with protecting society than the criminals.
Every day we see examples of society's problems in this regard.
Today, in the Montreal Matin, we can read at the top of the first page: Foul play suspected in ten-year old's death. If an adult contributed to his death I think this murder is vile. I resume my quotations from the paper: Restaurant owner mows down three motorcyclists. I am reading one newspaper only for if I were to take Le Devoir, La Presse, the Journal de Montreal, Le Jour or any other newspaper, other crimes would probably be reported.
This is why, I think, it is essential for policemen who have to investigate those crimes to have the necessary tools in order to work effectively.
It is all very well to have compassion on those who are charged with a crime, but let us be realistic. When teenagers are involved, I agree that that they should be treated with a little more clemency, in order to spare them a stigma they would keep for the rest of their life. Moreover, perhaps they did not make those mistakes. We are dealing with minors, young people of 16 or 17 with no police record. It is obvious that we must show discretion towards them.
However, as far as habitual criminals are concerned, people discharged from prison but condemned again for other serious crimes and still sought by police for murder,

rape, fraud or any other crime, it is important for the authorities to have the necessary tools to face the facts.
The bill reads as follows:
1. Subsection 2(3) of the Identification of Criminals Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(3) Where the person who has been subjected to the measurements, processes and operations under subsection (1)
(a) has been convicted of the offence
In other words, publication will be allowed only when the person is convicted. This is out of this world. Why not say then that taking steps to find a person and identify him or her will be allowed only when this person has been convicted?
According to the law we have now, signaletic cards are most important to find criminals. If we are to wait for a conviction, the best records will not be of any use.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that significant reserves must be made about Bill C-220. It is all right to have advanced ideas and to think and be a freethinker but we must not overdo it if individuals are to respect the administrative structures of this country. Authority must take action to be respected.
For those who have some notion of it, history teaches us that when progressive ideas get too strong in some country and when criminals are considered heroes instead of public enemies, this country begins losing prestige and to sink into decay.
Canada must avoid this. Furthermore, I think hon. members of the New Democratic Party should first show more respect for the life of unborn children by condemning abortion instead of fighting for it. It seems more important to me to protect these children's life than the criminals' who have no respect for their neighbour. In short, Mr. Speaker, I think this bill goes too far.
It is important that governments have a sense of justice so that each citizen feels happy to live in the country, so that nobody feels victimized. But we know that the freedom of one person ends where the freedom of the other begins; in other words, when one encroaches on the other's rights, the latter begin to lose his freedom and then he is less free, he does not feel free any more. I shall not say that we must favour criminals or crime, but to alleviate the measures against crime, which are definitely so light, is to favour crime. I think that it is against individual freedom. This bill does go against individual freedom since it prevents the police or the authorities concerned from taking the necessary steps to arrest those who prejudice the freedom of other people.
I do not think that this bill must be enacted or accepted by the Canadian people before decline has weakened us enough. It should thus be completely amended to give perhaps more justice to young people, as I said earlier.
As far as murderers, gangsters and criminals are concerned, I do not see very much where is the interest for society to protect them.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I had not intended to speak on this bill
April 22, 1974

until I came to the chamber and had an opportunity to listen to some of my colleagues participating in this private members' hour. I think that one could justifiably, on the basis of this afternoon's debate, suggest a change of name for the private members' hour to the "hypocrisy hour". Because in listening to the hon. member for Wind-sor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) filibustering his colleague's bill, though I realize that he did not really want to do so, one is provided with some justification for the suggestion that there is something radically wrong with the system, or procedures.
This bill is basically a very good and very enlightened bill, one which, I would like to state at the outset, I support. I share the feelings of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this is a good bill and that it should be sent forthwith to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for further study. So far as I can see, the provisions of this Identification of Criminals Act are often abused. Section 2, as the hon. member for Wind-sor-Walkerville pointed out, has a discretionary feature in that it states that:
Any person in lawful custody, charged with, or under conviction of an indictable offence, or who has been apprehended under the Extradition Act or the Fugitive Offenders Act, may be subjected ...
This is the part I would like to speak on for a moment or two. I have seen instances where police have in some cases, in my opinion, improperly invoked or tried to invoke the provisions of the Identification of Criminals Act when the circumstances made it clearly unnecessary to do so. I would like to point out to members in the House that on many occasions a criminal charge itself provides a punishment that can never be redressed. I am sure all hon. members realize that if, for example, a person is charged with a serious offence, comes to trial before a jury and is completely acquitted, on future occasions most people do not say: "There is John Jones, the man who was unjustly charged with robbery and was acquitted". They say: "There is that Jones fellow who was once up for robbery". This is the type of stigma that attaches to people even though they have been given a lawful trial and have been acquitted. I will not add any more on this point but I think it would be very interesting for the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) to issue guidelines and to make certain that this Identification of Criminals Act is not being abused by over zealous police officers across the country.
At this time I would also like to point out another area that bears looking into, and that is the department's policy regarding conditional discharges which, as I understand it-and many of my colleagues have brought this to my attention-is often opposed on principle by over zealous prosecuting officers who, in my opinion, often go against the spirit and intent of this government's policy by making it very difficult for defence counsel to utilize the very provisions that this government, very commendably, recently built into the Criminal Code.
At this time I do not want to be accused of speaking for too long because I would be doing what I am suggesting it is wrong for my colleagues to do, that is, talking out a very worthwhile piece of legislation that I for one would like to see referred to the committee. I would urge my colleagues to join me in this regard and not filibuster this bill, which
Identification of Criminals Act I think is one of the best I have seen come before the House during private members' hour recently.

Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to my colleague, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) when he introduced his bill.
I must say that from the very beginning, he seemed to me to be somewhat reticent, as though he wanted to plead in favour of this bill, but without conviction. I think he was quite sincere when he said that a burden should not be placed on some people for the rest of their lives unless they had appeared before the court, been formally charged and found guilty.
He has done some research on this bill, I am sure. He explained why we should not do these things, but I am still hesitant to accept his plea, regardless of his eloquence.
On a number of occasions, while considering private members' bills, he has looked into some situations which certainly appeared worthwhile to those who had brought them forward, but which seemed to show certain shortcomings after they had been scrutinized by other hon. members.
If the hon. member for Nipissing has himself listened to those who have accepted to participate in this debate, he must, I am sure, be entertaining some doubts by now.
The hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) went further and has denounced certain offences brought before the courts. As the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) was saying a while ago I think, it is not in any way permitted to interfere with the courts' work or with the carrying out of justice.
We have now reached the point where society has become quite belligerent. One hon. member was talking about it a few minutes ago. One has only to read newspapers, look at TV or listen to the radio to realize that people indulge in violence nearly everywhere.
If pieces of legislation are not brought in and discussed, if they are not thoroughly considered, we will feel somewhat remorseful. As I said earlier, there is violence in society.
The hon. member for Nipissing has pondered over the matter and suggested that if the person involved is not convicted, then his records should perhaps be destroyed. But it has also been pointed out during this debate that people may not be convicted for the offence which brought them into court, although they may have taken part in 15 or 20 other offences.
If the police or other investigating officers can be provided with some means that will enable them to identify the accused brought before the tribunal, then society will likely be relieved of a burden.
I think that the member for Nipissing was referring to the individual, but in terms of the community, of society, one must remember that a given measure may at one time or another make it difficult for some people.

April 22, 1974
Identification of Criminals Act
I agree fully with the hon. member when he suggests that one should not have to carry the burden of a charge if one is not guilty of any offence. On that point, I agree.
One other thing comes to mind: the police should be permitted to use whatever tools they have been provided with, but I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, the way certain business firms set up identification records by making use of fingerprinting, when they extend credit to people.
I do not think these practices are covered by the bill. And this does happen. People accused of no crime whatsoever have identification records set up against them merely for purposes of credit purchasing in stores. If these people resort to the identification process, why should we, in our wisdom, at least I think that the hon. member said it earlier, deprive the authorities that are trying to protect society of those tools? It is just as necessary.
I think we should devote to this problem much attention and much more time than we now have at our disposal.
Someone referred earlier to unions. Everyday we hear people say that unions harbour people who have criminal records or have committed offences and who are themselves responsible for the violence that exists. This has probably not been proved. I am sure that there are union people who have no twinges of conscience. They are doing a job and want to keep on developing the labour movement. However, some people who should not be there happen to worm their way in this movement. They are taking advantage of society and deprive other individuals of their freedom. If we think we can solve this problem by denying the necessary tools to those who are responsible for protecting society, we will do a disservice to society.
I am sure the hon. member for Nipissing wants to see his bill passed. I agree with my other colleagues who said that the main thrust of this bill was good. This measure is valid but I agree, however, with those of my colleagues who expressed much reservation in this regard.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say I am more concerned by the fact that we would deprive those who were asked to protect us of a tool which, in my view, is absolutely necessary. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-22, intituled Canadian Football Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it is incredible and even embarrassing for me to have to stand up in this House to speak on an issue dealing with football when this country is beset with so many critical issues affecting the lives of all Canadians.
Oh, oh!

I hear the hon. members opposite already making noises. 1 just want to say, Mr. Speaker, that last Thursday 1 gave them the opportunity to withdraw this bill when I asked for the unanimous consent of this House to move the following motion:
In view of the alarming growth of labour disputes already causing strikes in vital areas, and the inflationary spiral giving rise to them, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis): That this House welcomes the Prime Minister back from his vacation in Barbados and requests him to postpone the government's political football bill by bringing forward immediate legislation to alleviate the staggering inflationary problems which affect all Canadians.
As hon. members well know, this motion was defeated by members on the government side. I am not sure whether they opposed the part of the motion which welcomed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back from his vacation
April 22, 1974

or the portion to postpone the football bill in favour of more pressing legislation.
While the cost of living rises at a rate unprecedented in our history, the Liberal government still refuses to launch any attack to protect the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar. Nothing can be more ludicrous than this House sitting to discuss football while record breaking increases in the cost of living have once again been announced. It is incredible that while Canadians from one end of our country to the other reel in shock from food prices and housing costs, the Liberal government places before this House, as the priority item, legislation banning the World Football League from entering Toronto. At a time when every member of this House has received hundreds of letters urging the government to take action to control run away inflation, how can the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), in all honesty, even consider this is the time to discuss football?
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that were it not for the incompetence of the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), who has failed over and over again to stop this illegal postal strike we are presently faced with, doubtless many more letters would have reached the offices of each and every member. Yet the government has chosen to force football legislation on to the House, despite the pressing priorities facing each and every Canadian in so many other fields.
Not only does the government not have its priorities straight in introducing legislation, but even in the legislation before us its priorities are not in the right order. If we are to get involved in sports in this country, then surely we should not be putting the emphasis on professional sports but rather on the development of amateur athletes, as well as the over-all physical fitness activities of all Canadians.
The federal government's purpose-in sports and fitness as in everything else-should be to help all Canadians to enjoy richer, fuller and more satisfying lives. The government cannot achieve that purpose by concentrating on, and indeed emphasizing the importance of, professionalism, as it is with this bill. Our most important national resource is the youth of this country, and, as with any other resource, a national development policy must be initiated, with incentives for participation heading the list.
I made it very clear during the debate on the Combines Investigation Act, Bill C-7, that not only do I believe that for us to debate this bill at this critical time is wrong, but that the bill itself will not fulfil the purpose for which it was intended, namely to protect the Canadian Football League.
I would be the last person wishing to see the demise of the Canadian Football League in any way whatsoever. On the contrary, it would be my wish to see greater opportunities afforded the youth of this country by encouraging even greater Canadian participation in the Canadian Football League than that proposed in the bill before us. On the other hand, a recent statement made by a great ex-football star and great Canadian, Russ Jackson, who said that if the Canadian Football League cannot stand on its own feet then it should not stand at all, should be considered.
Canadian Professional Football
Be that as it may, what is of prime concern to me, and should be of prime concern to every member of this House, is that the youth of this country be afforded every conceivable opportunity not only to participate in sports and become physically, as well as mentally, proficient, but be afforded as well the opportunity to participate in professional sports in Canada regardless of league. They should be protected in their choice of team and league. Indeed the government has introduced legislation to this effect. Allow me to quote section 32.3(1) (b) of the Combines Investigation Act amending Bill C-7:
Every one who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with another person
(b) to limit unreasonably the opportunity for any other person to negotiate with and, if agreement is reached, to play for the team or club of his choice in a professional or amateur league
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable on conviction to
imprisonment for two years.
Naturally, we would not want to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) imprisoned for a two year period. However, if he had been imprisoned in the past, then we would not be faced with this ridiculous bill that we have to stand here and debate at this time.
However, I personally approve in principle of the sports sections of the combines investigation bill, which ironically is in total contradiction to the bill before us. We have, on the one hand, the government submitting a bill which it alleges will stimulate competition. On the other hand, we have the same government introducing a bill to prevent competition. If this bill before us becomes law in its present form, we will be the first country in the world outlawing international sports competition in a certain field and will become the laughing stock of the sports world.
Has this government forgotten that this country was built on free enterprise? Has this government forgotten that this country was built on competition?
I hope so.
I hear the NDP yelling "I hope so." They are against free enterprise. The reason I escaped with my family from Czechoslovakia was to get away from guys like that.
Hear, hear!

Since when does any government have the right to dictate to the people of Canada what they can or cannot see in professional sports, or for that matter in any form of entertainment?
Where was the federal government when the World Hockey Association entered the Canadian sports scene? Where was the concern for the advancement of opportunities for the youth of this country? Why did the government fail to provide safeguards and encouragement to the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association, and why are there no proposed changes in this bill relating to hockey, truly our national sport? Why has football been singled out as a target of intervention? Would it not have been reasonable to expect the government to take a firm stand on the
1650

Canadian Professional Football protection of this sport long before the World Football League was even contemplated? Certainly safeguards are needed to keep our amateur junior teams viable.
Possibly the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) interfered in football at this stage of the game to set a precedent for Montreal. The ultimate use of the Olympic stadium after the 1976 Olympic Games by a National Football League team is a great possibility. It is a possibility that has been rumoured. Even Mayor Drapeau has suggested on numerous occasions in the past that it might be his wish to bring a National Football League team into Montreal. If this were to happen, then unfortunately the Montreal Alouettes, which do not get the crowds they deserve, would be hurt financially a great deal and, therefore, the Canadian Football League may suffer.
While we are on this subject of the protection of other sports, may I ask whether the government should not consider obtaining revenue for amateur sport development from foreign organizations such as professional ice shows? And I am speaking specifically about American ice shows, professional basketball teams, professional basketball players or golfers who come into this country. Why are we not concerned about them? They come into this country and continue to drain off all our top talents without contributing to Canadian amateur organizations which have invested their time and money in developing these athletes.
As I have previously outlined, I am opposed to this bill as it in no way serves its purpose of protecting the Canadian Football League. I believe that contrary to my wishes, however, the bill will pass into committee stage, at which time I hope hon. members will seriously consider options which will truly Canadianize professional sports in Canada but will at the same time allow foreign teams to play in Canada under certain conditions and with the approval of the local populace and their civic authorities.
Some of the options or amendments which in my opinion should be considered in professional sports in Canada-and I stress professional sports, not just professional football-are the following. First, to have the civic authority in the designated area consent to the foreign team operating in their area. Why should we not let the people of a certain area decide what they want to charge and what they want to participate in instead of meddling with business that is not even national or interprovincial business?
Second, the foreign team should guarantee to the satisfaction of a Canadian professional sports league concerned to save harmless the Canadian league that there will be no decrease in equalization payments based upon the sharing of gate receipts within the Canadian league due to the operation of the foreign team in the designated area.
Third, the foreign team, at the direction of, and in an amount determined by, the Canadian league, should contribute monies toward the support of the amateur league in Canada.
Fourth, the foreign team, and all other teams within that foreign league, should honour the contracts of players on teams operated by members of the Canadian league and not interfere with the regulation by the Canadian league

of the recruitment and allocation of players within that league.
Fifth, the foreign team should undertake not to permit any game in which it participates in Canada to be broadcast in any area where such broadcast would, in the opinion of the Canadian league, adversely affect the gate, broadcasting or other receipts of a game in which two teams operated by members of the Canadian league are participating.
In this manner we would give the Canadian Football League, if we want to be specific and talk on football, the right to veto any particular team in any one city, rather than give the federal government authority to close the door on international competition. International competition has been the basis of all sports competition the world over. This government is now trying to stop that. It is trying to set a precedent with one sport. That has never before been seen in the world. In this manner also, Canadian professional sports would be protected to a greater extent than by totally banning international competition in a specific sport.
I said I would be brief and that I am embarrassed to be discussing football at this time, with all the problems we have arising from the inflationary situation. In closing, let me just say that, in retrospect, the Minister of National Health and Welfare should have closed his remarks in Regina last February with the following statement: "I know that you believe you understand what you think I said, but I am not sure you realize that what you heard is not what I meant."

When a Member of Parliament sees a piece of bad, ill-timed legislation, he ought not to sit in his seat because some football player on the other side says he should. I did not come to this House to give what might be considered tacit support to ill-timed, bad legislation. I say to the government in all seriousness that there is nothing which indicates more clearly its lack of relevance with respect to the problems of the day than the pig-headed, wrong-headed effort it is making in connection with this legislation. Particularly is this so today, when I note that 2,000 employees of Air Canada have been laid off, inflation is rampant, and the postal unions are so disgusted with the archaic and dinosaur-like methods of the government in bargaining with the Civil Service that they are prepared to withhold their services. This is a time when the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) should be directing his attention toward mediation, instead of publishing a stupid advertisement two days running which only inflames the situation.
That is typical of a government which has chosen to bring forward a bill of the kind before us, ignoring the national issues which are concerning our people. We do not intend to be party to that kind of irrelevancy and ineptitude. If ever there was a monument to government ineptitude, it is the present bill introduced at this time.
A great deal of reference has been made to the views of Mr. Russell Jackson, a Canadian who made his way in football without assistance from the government opposite or from any government. Mr. Jackson's name has been used in this chamber on many occasions. He put his opinion clearly when he said:
I just think that if the CFL is too weak to face this kind of competition, we are going to lose it eventually anyway. If it can't compete without government legislation, then some other league, some other team such as the Northmen, or some other sport entirely, will knock it out.
That is a statement by a man who knows Canadian football. It might be pointed out again that the legislation before us will not help the Canadian Football League. Many reasons have been advanced in the course of the debate and I shall not repeat them. Not a single speaker from the government side, including the minister, has shown us how this legislation will help Canadian football. I am not prepared to take the government's word for it because this is the same government which told us there was a fuel shortage in Canada and then went on to make a wasteful purchase of Roumanian oil, after which we found out there was not a shortage at all.
The people I represent in this House say there are two real issues which concern us. First, there is the irrelevance of the government's action at this time. They say it is not proper, in the face of the urgent problems now before the country, that parliament should be dealing with football. I concur in that view. The second thing they say is that parliament has more important things to do.
Right! So sit down and we will vote on it.

As a matter of propriety, parliament ought not to be injecting itself into the field of professional sport. That is the second consideration. They say the government does have a mandate with respect to amateur
Canadian Professional Football sport, a role to play in terms of helping to secure the participation of the greatest possible number of Canadians in sport and fitness programs. The appearance of this bill, and the pressure the government has applied, indicate how it has failed in carrying out that mandate.
There is a lot to be done in the field of amateur sport. All of us, I believe, have a feeling of gratification, a sense of obligation toward those who engage in the coaching of young players, and a sense of pride in the achievement of those who take part in amateur sports. Those who work with boys and girls, helping them to participate, are the unsung heroes of sport in Canada. These people are being neglected as a result of the government's preoccupation with a field in which it has no real reason to be active. Think of the shortage of playgrounds in Canada, the shortage of equipment, the fact that there are not enough arenas.
When I think of the great value there is in figure skating, soccer, lacrosse and hockey on the amateur level, and of the thousands of young people who are involved in these sports, and weigh tnis against tne preoccupation of the Minister ot National Healtn and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) with professional sport, I begin to wonder how the priorities of the government are arranged. Where is its sense of relevancy? Where is its sense of urgency? I come to the conclusion that the government is out of touch.
What is the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs?

I think that was one of the most thoughtful speeches I have heard in respect of the elements which are or ought to be the minds of members in respect of this bill.
That hon. member laid out six very important points which ought to be considered by hon. members, some of which I have touched upon. He said that this bill could not by any stretch of the imagination be construed as an attempt to defend anything cultural. He called that a phony aspect of the considerations of this bill. He said that this legislation would be futile in respect to protecting the Canadian Football League, which every member of this House wants to see flourish. The point is that this bill will not protect that league. He went on to say, and I think this is a most important part of his speech, that this government is denying to Canadians the basic right of viewing sports in the manner they wish.
If you look at the restrictive provisions of this bill you will find that they are restrictions which you cannot find in any other piece of legislation. All in all, the bill is bad. It is an irrelevant piece of legislation which will not carry out the object the framers of the bill would like everyone to believe it will carry out. The bill encroaches upon the rights of Canadians in respect of the field of entertainment in a way no other government has ever seen fit to do. The bill puts this parliament into a position where it is invading a field it has no right to be in.
As pointed out by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey), there is a real question as to the constitutionality of the powers of this bill, and there is certainly a question as to the propriety of the powers it purports to give to the government.
Lastly, and perhaps most importantly, in the face of all the problems confronting this country, with people crying out for a reasonable choice of housing at a reasonable cost, people asking the government to devote its priorities to land banking in order to increase the supply of serviced land and to engage in a dramatic program of servicing acres of land so there will be adequate land for housing, in an age when the people of Canada are saying to this government that because of inflation they do not know where they are going to be next year and do not know whether labour contracts negotiated this year will be relevant, at a time when the whole system of bargaining in respect of the Public Service is breaking down and becoming irrelevant because it is slow, cumbersome and unresponsive to needs, at a time when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has indicated his department is in difficulties in supplying hopper cars for the movement of grain in Canada, when his airline, for whatever reason, is not functioning and is tying up transportation, and at a time when post office workers have decided, rightly or

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-22 I think I should first say that truth is indeed often stranger than fiction.
God, I wish I had said that.
You said it the first time.

We might take as an example last Thursday. The government was then faced with inflation running at 10.4 per cent per annum and with wage earners who had had their purchasing power eroded by 1.8 per cent in 1973. The government was faced with postal workers who were tying up the mail from coast to coast while airport firefighters were disrupting air travel at Canada's main airports. The government was also faced with 2,100 air controllers threatening what the air controllers call a total airline shutdown, which is similar to what 136 seaway pilots had succeeded in doing in respect to the St. Lawrence Seaway. There were reports of rising labour militancy across the land, including violence on the picket line with 400 Toronto food workers struck.
Yet on that Thursday, late in the evening the government chose, from among 17 items of government business that could have been debated, to ask parliament to debate this bill concerned with who should play football in Toronto, who should own the team that plays the game, and what league the team should be in. Mr. Speaker, in asking for a debate on the football bill the government had to move the matter from 12th position of priority to the first position of priority. The government had to move it ahead of items such as a bill to help control rising commodity prices, which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), if he were here I know would agree we have assured him will receive speedy passage in this House when the government introduces it. It had to be moved ahead of a bill to protect human health from contamination in the environment. This football bill had to be moved ahead of another one which might even have brought more competition into our banking system in this country.
Having decided to introduce the bill, after one hour and five minutes in which he explained the bill to the House the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) then asked the House to pass the bill speedily with as few debaters as possible. Then the same Minister of National Health and Welfare, apparently a little worried that the bill might not pass, was very quick to claim that the matter was a "gut" issue, but of course not a matter of confidence. I found it very interesting that a minister introducing a bill would show so little confidence himself in its passage that he would hasten to say to members that, in his view, it would not be a matter of confidence if the bill should be voted down by members of the House.
When this legislation was first proposed, and indeed after the bill was introduced, I did not intend to speak on the matter since I felt it would be well covered by members from the government and the opposition.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
I say that because I believe that many in this country enjoy football, and certainly I am one. I have attended Canadian football games in Ottawa, Toronto, Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg and Hamilton; and I have attended many Grey Cup games, including some held in Hamilton, Ottawa and Toronto. I even attended that famous Grey Cup game when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), wearing his Dracula hat and cape, was present. It may be that that is the instance when it dawned on the Prime Minister that this thing called the Grey Cup promoted national unity.
But after listening to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and after reading the bill I could see only two reasons why the government was advancing this bill as top priority. The first was that it seemed to me that they had decided that they must make some token gesture to indicate their concern with foreign investment or involvement in this country, and they felt that perhaps what might get the best press for them was to present this football legislation and shake their fist at the Yankee and say: Go home, Yankee, leave our football as it is.
The second reason I felt that the minister and his government were advancing the legislation was that there was vindictiveness towards those who were proposing to bring a new league into Canada and establish a new football team in Toronto. I say that because all of us here remember that only very recently another international football league played in Toronto, the Continental League. They had a team in Toronto, namely the Rivals. I do not recall this government or its predecessor uttering the slightest murmur that they felt that somehow that entry into the Toronto market was objectionable.
So I am suggesting that there are possibly only two basic reasons why this government is virtually using closure to try to get this bill through the House: one is the token objection that they wish to make toward foreign investment in this country; the second is the vindictive streak in this government toward the promoters of the foreign team.
Hear, hear!

These are my preliminary views. I wanted to look up the history of football, so I went to the library and read two or three books on the Grey Cup and the CFL. I would strongly recommend that before the little trained seals across the way continue to support this legislation they read some of the history of our Canadian Football League and the Grey Cup itself. I think they might find it interesting to know that although we call it a Canadian game, in fact the game was derived from England. It evolved as a result of a league between McGill and Harvard. So right at its inception we find that it was in fact a Canadian-United States activity.
I also found that the Grey Cup was in fact made in England and exported here. I found that the Toronto Argonauts, who, as they say, are proud to play under the double blue, got the light blue from Cambridge and the dark blue from Oxford. So here we have what I would regard as not a truly Canadian sport in the sense that it

was developed and inspired by Canadians; it is a sport which in fact evolved in Canada from its predecessor in England, and which has subsequently been exported from Canada to the United States where they developed it still further to what is now known as the American game. I think we should all realize, first of all, that what we call Canadian football, about which the Minister of National Health and Welfare was so emotional, is in fact an evolving sport and one which will continue to evolve.
Having traced that background I think I should refer to what I regard as this government's token gesture. To do this I think it is only fair to review very quickly the extent of foreign ownership in this country.
If the government is indeed alarmed about foreign involvement in our business world and in our culture, surely it is cognizant of the figures made available under the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act which came out in March, 1974. Hon. members will note that the total assets of foreign controlled corporations in Canada were approximately $50 billion in 1970, and in one year they went up $4.5 billion to $54.5 billion. Then we find that the profits of the same corporations-I am referring to the corporations controlled by foreign interests in Canada- rose between 1970 and 1971 from $3.5 billion to something over $4 billion, an increase of $582 million in one year, over half a billion dollars. I think it is interesting to note that over $2 billion on that amount-$2.2 billion-was actually paid to the foreign owners of those businesses in 1971. This sum made up of $791 million in dividends, $523 million in interest, and $925 million in business services such as management contracts.
Let me summarize. In 1971, foreign controlled corporations in the non-financial industries in Canada, while they accounted for only 4 per cent of all the corporations in Canada in terms of numbers, represented 37 per cent of the assets, 44 per cent of the equity, 38 per cent of the sales, 46 per cent of the profits, and 47 per cent of the positive taxable income in Canada. To which foreigners am I referring? Specifically, the report points out that in 1971 total payments to foreigners in the United States was $1,599 million.
I have been referring to a Canadian publication on the extent of foreign ownership in the business world in Canada. I would draw attention once again to the fact that this publication only came out in March, 1974 and that the most up to date figures given were those for 1971. It is regrettable that in order to get more recent figures concerning foreign investment in Canada I have to turn to the International Economic Report of the President of the United States.
In his report of February, 1974 he gives the American version of what they are receiving from Canada. We find that in 1972 the investment income receipts in the American books from Canada are shown as $2 billion. On top of that are royalties received by the Americans of $.4 billion. In 1973-and I again emphasize these are American presidential figures because Canadian figures are not provided-the investment income receipts had jumped to $2.5 billion, another $500 million increase, and royalties stayed at the $.4 billion level.

I mention that bit of background, Mr. Speaker, because I suggest that this government has not done anything effectively to reverse the foreign ownership of industry in Canada. In fact, in introducing and speaking on this bill the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) did not even know the name of the bill that his government passed concerning foreign investment in this country. If you check Hansard you will find that he referred to it as the "foreign policy review act" and took great credit for the fact that this was something that was somehow going to counteract foreign investment in Canada. The correct name is the Foreign Investment Review Act. I think that shows how lightly the cabinet weigh the various pieces of legislation that come before it. It may in fact be a freudian slip, that reference to the foreign policy review; undoubtedly their foreign policy does need review.
I have touched in a general sense on the impact of foreign investment in Canada but I should like to be more specific, Mr. Speaker. After listening to the debate on Friday I went home on the aeroplane to Toronto and for the first time in many years looked through a copy of Reader's Digest, that fine Canadian journal to which this government has given such favourable tax treatment in order to keep it in Canada.

In answer to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), there was not only George Hees' article, but on the inside front page I found an article by none other than the hon. Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis). I found it most interesting that the article was entitled "Understanding is Half the Battle". In it he recited various things that the Reader's Digest had done that he thinks are commendable. Specifically he says "I commend the magazine", and he concludes by saying that we must remember those ringing words of Maurice Strong, who said "There is 'only one earth'".
Mr. Speaker, surely it is an odd situation that we have a government that says that national unity is at stake if certain people are playing football in Toronto this year or next year, yet apparently feels there is no particular reason to change the favourable tax treatment for the American publication Reader's Digest. I have seen some balance sheets and sales figures of professional football teams in Canada. I know what they earn and I know what their sales are. Reader's Digest sales in 1973 were $28.5 million and their profit was $1,757,000 after tax. Their shareholders' equity of $5,534,000 is larger than the revenue of the entire league. I can assure hon. members that it is probably three times, maybe four times, the size of the entire league.
What can we draw from this odd and apparent contradiction? Why should the government be so concerned about who plays football while seeming to have so little concern about foreign ownership in this country generally and specifically about such things as Reader's Digest- which in fact is even commended for its fine activities in Canada?
Let me give the House another example of how one who comes from the general area of Toronto finds the priorities

of this government so odd. Some of us may have heard of the Process Church of the Final Judgment, which is often referred to as the Satanists. As we know, that church had its origin in the United States and its followers decided to come over the border. We did not see any bill rushed through this House to stop them. In fact, we found the reverse; they were able to pick up a LIP grant of $40,093. I would imagine, Mr. Speaker, that most members, like myself, sometimes stroll along the Sparks Street mall. If they do, they may be approached by one of the disciples of the Process Church. I would suggest they ask where they receive their greatest assistance in Canada. If any hon. member speaks to the same disciple that I spoke to, he will be rather startled to hear that it was the federal government that gave them their greatest lift in Canada with a LIP grant.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we have a government that sees nothing wrong with giving grants to a foreign religious cult that wishes to come into Canada, and which on the other hand gets up so tight that it asks the parliament of Canada, in face of all the other problems in this country, to give priority to a bill to decide who should play football.
I noticed that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was hovering around me. He may wish to speak; I am not sure. Now dealing with sports, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to interfere with "Boom-Boom Knowles". There is an explosion coming, I understand. In fact, he has even told me to be careful what I say now!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We are not worried.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is pretty obvious why we have this bill before us at this time. In addition to the reasons I have mentioned I think this is perhaps a very easy meeting ground for the poor, tired old government that is so rife with indecision.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Like the unity of the Conservative Party- tremendous.

What better meeting ground for the left wing of the government, of which presumably the Minister of National Health and Welfare feels he is part, and the right wing of that party, members such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). Here we have a business proposition and a sports activity blending into one, allowing the right in that party to meet the left and advance something with some type of accord.
Let me be specific. I believe the government should not be giving the priority it is to this bill. We have more serious matters to deal with than a football bill.
Hear, hear!

The government must accept full responsibility for what we are debating in this House at any time. If they wish to bring in meaningful legislation or, better still, if they would like to name an opposition day to test the confidence of this House, I will be the first to say let's get on with it.
Hear, hear!

Second, I suggest the government has no place trying to regulate professional entertainment, which is all that professional sports is in Canada at the present time. I suggest that likely the bill before us is not constitutional. In this regard I agree with the excellent speech by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). If the government thinks it is constitutional, exactly where do they get the federal power under the British North America Act?
There is a right for people to choose their own form of entertainment. It may be that, contrary to the government's contention, a Bassett knows what people in Toronto want more than a Lalonde from Montreal. It is no accident that CFTO, the television station, is the number one station for viewers in the Toronto area while the CBC ranks number five.
It was suggested-and surely the minister must have been laughing when he said it-that this bill ties in with national unity. I guess he had been watching the TV series "The National Dream". He referred to such things as the building of the railways. If this is the thread holding our country together, I suggest it is a very, very fragile union that we have in this country.
This bill does not do what the minister should be doing, that is helping amateur sport in this country. When I decided to speak on this bill, I spoke with Canadian and American football players who are now active in the Canadian Football League. I now have the firm conviction that the number one thing that is wrong with Canadian football at the present time is that there is not enough assistance to ensure that players right down to the lowest grades are given the opportunity to learn and play the game that is given those in the United States.
Without mentioning his name, one chap who is perhaps one of the leading players with the Toronto Argonauts told me he played the game in the United States from grade six, and that at the present time they have coaches in their public schools encouraging and coaching the American children to play football. That is how to learn the game. That is how we are so eminent in the world of hockey. If we wish to be eminent in football, it would be more practical for the minister to be suggesting that kind of legislation, rather than fretting over who is going to put on a sports spectacular in Toronto.
Although the point has been made, I think it should be made again that the Canadian Football League is not national. Its activity stops at Montreal. We should bear in mind that almost 25 per cent of the Canadian population lives east of Montreal.
I again refer to how somebody in the Toronto area may look at this. For example, my constituency takes in part of the region of York which would like to build a dome stadium. They have proposed a site and have plans to dig. They have not had one iota of encouragement from the federal government to get on with this development. Surely that is an interesting contrast with the $500 million the government has put up for the Olympics in Montreal. Dealing again with the Toronto situation, one of the reasons given by the federal authorities as to why we are not entitled to help for a dome stadium is that it might be used for professional football.

I have attempted in the few minutes available to me to touch on what I think are the pertinent points in this bill. I urge members to vote against the bill. I intend to do so. My party intends to do so. I can assure hon. members that given an opportunity, as has been outlined in our policy papers which were approved at our convention, we will bring in more meaningful legislation to help amateur sport in this country and to ensure that resource industry companies and companies in general will be restored in ownership to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill, not with the intention of prolonging the debate but to say some things that I think need saying.
This bill has stirred up a great deal of public controversy. Until the mail in this country stopped, this bill accounted for at least 10 of the letters I received a day, and for numerous telegrams and telephone calls both to my office here and my constituency office on the weekend at all times of day. This bill has stirred my people up to a great extent. It has wrought controversy throughout my constituency on both sides of the question. I will go into that controversy later.
This bill is very much like one we had last year in connection with capital punishment. It hits at the roots of people. It attacks the "gut" issues. Members opposite are afraid to talk about it. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) is afraid to talk about it, as is the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Ontario is rising on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if it is not asking too much in this House, individual members should behave with a certain degree of responsibility. I certainly am not afraid to speak about this. I have spoken about it across the country. However, I am prepared to vote on it, which is the very function we have in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I should not comment on the activities of other members in this House, but if their mail is anything like mine, and I know it is, they have a duty to their constituents to say where they stand and why they are voting. This is not a clean yes or no issue. It is very complicated. It is an issue that strikes at the very guts of all of us. That is why we have to stand up and speak. That is why every member in this House should stand up. It is why this bill should be set aside until the situation in this country clears up a bit. We should not be talking about this bill at a time when we have an increase of 1 per cent a month inflation. The Post Office is not working-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, sit down so that we can talk about those things.

The bill should be deferred so that we can consider it dispassionately, so that members can air the feelings of their constituents and explain to their
Canadian Professional Football constituents what the bill is all about. We cannot be expected to vote on a bill without setting out the reasons why we voted and what it is all about. It is imperative that we analyse the feelings of our constituents. That is the least we owe them. They have the right to expect this of us as members of the parliament of Canada. It is not fair for an hon. member to hide behind the curtain, to refuse to speak. He cannot escape his responsibility by not voting or by keeping quiet because some party official or whip has been on his back.
At least we are not split on this issue like you are.

It is not an easy problem. It is one which raises the whole question of freedom. It is an issue on which members of parliament should stand up and be heard. A government which brings forward a bill of this kind, puts on two speakers and then says "Vote, vote, vote!" is not responding to the needs of the people of Canada as it should be required to respond.
There are two issue here, and they are in conflict. The first is the right of a free people to see what they want to see, to play what they want to play and to hear what they want to hear. The other issue involves the national unity of Canada and the extent to which football unifies the country. And it does unify the country. We cannot forget that there is a big brother south of the border. These are the two issues before the House and they must be spoken about. This is what parliament is for; parliament is a speaking place. Gut issues are before us, yet members say "Vote, vote, vote, vote!" That is no answer to their constituents.
I took a poll in my riding. I do that often through the mailing system we have. The questionnaire asked two questions: Are you in favour of (a) preventing the expansion of American professional football into Canada? To this, 44 per cent of my constituents said, yes, 32 per cent said no, and 23 per cent were undecided. Then I reversed the question. I asked: (b) Are you in favour of allowing American football into Canada? To this question, 39 per cent said yes, 37 per cent said no, and 23 per cent were undecided. As hon. members will appreciate, it is almost a 50-50 issue.
We get opinions in letters and telegrams from people right across the country, people who are worried about the identity of Canada, people who are worried about whether we are creating the kind of country Laurier talked about at the beginning of this century, people who are worried about the freedom of Canadians as individuals to do what they want to do-play a sport, listen to a sport, see a sport. These are gut issues, and that is why the country is divided. That is why members opposite ha"e a duty to speak.
The question is: Do we need legislation to protect the Canadian Football League? When we look at the league we find that 80 per cent of the stars are American. It is rumoured that the ownership of at least one team may be American. It is rumoured that every coach in the league is American. The bill before us permits 45 per cent of the players to be American this year and 40 per cent next year. This is Canadian football and we have to make sure that Canadian football is protected.

This is not a positive bill, a bill which does something for Canadian football. It does nothing for Canadian football at all. This is a piece of legislation which says: If you play in a foreign league, you go to jail for two years. Football is an important national sport, but we must remember that it is only played actively as a professional sport west of the island of Montreal. As I say, it is a unifying sport, but is it so important that the government of Canada should be making rules to control it and not rules with respect to every other professional sport?
Is this a subject which should be looked at now, a time when economic exigencies are threatening the country, or should such consideration be deferred to a more apt occasion? Is it really necessary to make sure that the Northmen are thrown out of Canada on the grounds that if they were not, poor old Canada, and national sport in Canada, would disintegrate? I suggest the raison d'etre of this bill will not stand up to serious examination.
The Toronto market is more than capable of supporting two professional football teams. After all, we have an affluent market of at least four million people and there are already many competing athletic events as well as other cultural activities taking place simultaneously in Toronto. The entry of the Toronto Northmen playing in a foreign league will not mean a thing to the market, any more than if we organized a new soccer team, a new lacrosse team, another hockey team, a professional basketball team, or even more professional tennis stars. This really would not matter because the market is far larger than any which could be satisfied by the Canadian Football League at the present time or in the foreseeable future.
This bill is not really going to do a thing for Canadian unity, but it will deprive the people of the greater Toronto and Ontario area of the right to look at what they want to see when they want to see it, or if they are prepared to pay for the ticket to see it.
When the minister introduced this bill he waxed long about the CPR as the national dream, about the CBC and how the Conservative party was responsible in the original instance for forming that corporation, and he talked about national unity and national identity. He did not mention the penalty of two years in jail when he talked about national unity in relation to these other national things.
What are we talking about here? We are talking about a football team. We are talking about one football team in one city competing in an international league. Perhaps this is just a continental league, but it is a league about which we are talking. What audacity to compare that with activities in Canada such as building a pipeline, a seaway, a railway, a radio network or the unity of this country! As I suggested earlier, that borders on the ridiculous.
This arrangement Mr. Bassett has with the WFL is an arrangement whereby he has the right to operate one team in the World Football League in Canada. He has given the minister the assurance that there will be only one WFL team in Canada. What the minister is suggesting is that the city of Toronto cannot support one football team playing in international competition, and that if that one

football team plays in Toronto the gate receipts of the CFL will be so tremendously damaged that the whole CFL will fall apart and the Grey Cup will be used as an ash can. That is what he is saying. Does that not sound ridiculous when compared with the CBC, the CPR, the trans-Canada pipeline, the Seaway and all those things Canadians have accomplished through good times, bad times, depression and war? He says the CFL will fall apart if we have one team located in Toronto competing in an international league. He says the whole country will fall apart and national unity will be destroyed forever.
What about this international league? When people talk about professional baseball in this country they cheer the Montreal Expos because they play big league baseball in the big leagues. Canadians who are interested in big league baseball like to see the Montreal Expos play in other cities throughout the United States. We have a team playing baseball in international competition, so what would be wrong with our having a team playing football in international competition-and I emphasize, only one team in Canada? The minister says this is going to destroy the country; it will destroy Regina, wipe out Winnipeg and visit disaster upon Edmonton, Calgary and Vancouver. Such nonsense! Can Canadians not go beyond their borders and win games in New York, Atlanta and other cities in the United States, and perhaps even lose some as well? What is wrong with Canadians going into international competition? The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) spoke earlier about this.
This is the first time the government has said: Thou shalt not enter a league in Canada, competing internationally in any league in another country. That is what this bill is; it is a "Thou shalt not" bill.
Hon. members opposite suggest that we should keep quiet, not speak too often, let this bill come to a vote and pass quickly. They do not want to talk about it because they know in their very heart of hearts that this bill is not right and should not pass.
Show me a Liberal with a heart. I don't know any of them.

The part of this bill that bothers me most is Clause 6. If this was a bill designed to encourage Canadians by providing that any professional football team in Canada must have so many Canadians on its roster and no more than so many foreigners on its coaching or playing staff, I would not be quite so upset. This bill provides that any Canadian who plays for a team playing football in any foreign league in Canada as defined-and it refers to Canadian or American football-will be subject to two years in jail. That is the iniquitous part of this bill. If this bill, following its marvellous preamble, went on to show some method by which growing young Canadians would be encouraged to play football and be given more opportunity, that would be pretty good.
If this bill provided that the CFL must have teams in London, Halifax, Quebec City and Charlottetown, that might be a good thing too. But this bill provides nothing of the kind. This bill confirms the fact that the Canadian Football League is entitled to continue to have at least 15 American players on its roster, providing that is not more than 40 per cent of the authorized playing group. It does

not say anything about giving more opportunity to young athletes, and it does nothing to encourage amateur sports in Canada. This is a "Thou shalt not" bill, and this government is used to that kind of bill.
Last session when the matter of foreign control was raised this government produced the foreign control takeover bill, another "Thou shalt not" bill. Every time we on this side of the House suggested that there should be taxing incentives and better arrangements for banking facilities for Canadians to take over Canadian enterprises in Canada, hon. members opposite did not want any part of it.
This is a "Thou shall not" approach to Canadian identity. As a member of this party I say that if we are to build an identity in Canada we will never build it by two years in jail. That is the approach we have had from this government in connection with Canadian identity. We need a positive approach which gives Canadians encouragement to do things, to build Canada. There is no attempt to build Canada in a statute which prohibits and controls, which makes Canadians look inward, which provides that Canadians shall not compete in international competition. That is the nature of this bill and this is the reason it must fail. It does nothing for Canadian identity. It does not build up Canada. It is a two-years-in-jail bill. That the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) should let that pass I am surprised.
Much has been said about whether this bill has constitutional validity. I have said before that I am only a country lawyer and do not know very much about this, but it strikes me that any sport that can be broadcast on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation must not be a sport that is criminal in nature. So to ban the playing of that sport as a crime while at the same time allowing the broadcasting of that sport on a national television network owned by the people of Canada must perforce mean either that the government is full of criminals or that the sport is fine. So this bill cannot stand on the basis of the criminal law or the peace, order and good government provision.
Is there likely to be insurrection if this bill should not pass and the Northmen do in fact play? Are we to destroy peace, order and good government if we have football in Canada? Clearly not. There are two members on the government side who are law professors and one on this side, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey). I am surprised the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGui-gan) has not stood up in this House and given a legal opinion in this case. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), a former dean of a law school, has not given his legal opinion on the validity of this bill. Clearly the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the hon. member for St. Paul's and a number of others have called into question the validity of this statute.
Surely it is incumbent upon competent people with legal talent on the government benches to say that they really believe concerning the validity of this statute. Yet we have not heard from them. They do not want to speak about it because they are pretty well convinced we are right when we say that, and they do not want to embarrass

The evidence is that there would be no damage to national unity in Canada as a result of the non-passage of this bill or as a result of the Northmen playing football in Canada. There is no evidence that people will really be injured, that the cities of Regina, Winnipeg and Calgary will fall apart. All we have is suspicion. All we have is an issue which is pretty small, which really does not go to the heart of what this House should be discussing at a time when we have the Post Office and the air line out of commission. This bill should be tabled by this government. It should be brought up again for future debate, but it should be tabled now so the government can get on with the urgent business of running the economy of Canada instead of messing around with football.

Mr. Speaker, it has been evident all day and all evening not only that the government want this debate truncated but that we know why they want silence. They have much to be silent about. They certainly have a desire to be silent about the way they have bumbled the economy of this country, bumbled the issue of the cost of living and now have bumbled this. But this can be seen in a tragic light when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) gives priority to a bill such as this at a time when there are so many things vital to the future of the Canadian people, so many things on which we would welcome legislation and direction from the minister and his colleagues. However, about these things he and they have been silent.
We wish, for example, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would give us an opportunity to debate with him the present inadequate funding of medical research in this country and the way increases for the Medical Research Council are not even keeping pace with the cost of living.
We wish the minister would give us an opportunity to deliberate upon the inadequate funding of institutions that fight alcohol and drug abuse. The government takes in hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue from the sale of alcohol, yet provides only a token amount of this for education to combat it. We wish, for example, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, would bring in a program on the subject and challenge of traffic fatalities, which are now threatening 200,000 potential years of lost life annually. We wish there were some presentation from the minister on what could be done to increase government funding for research in respect to heart disease, cancer, mental health problems, aging and many other priority items of the Canadian people. When the Minister of National Health and Welfare gives priority to a bill such as this we must think that he is now becoming the Mr. Bumble of Canadian politics. Here is another example of how this government has bumbled without leadership and direction in so many areas and so many challenges.
Who can believe in a government that produces legislation of this kind at this time? Indeed the only explanation that can be given is that this must be the creation of those so-called strategists who devised such incredible things as the 60 days of decision during the 1963 election and now have conceived this brainchild.
27451-42*

April 22, 1974
